measurement.happened:
The dominant story of the week in the United States was the midterm elections and their aftershocks. On November 4, Democrats delivered what multiple outlets called a 'blue tsunami' or 'blue wave,' flipping both the House and the Senate in what the Financial Times called 'the beginning of the end of the age of Trump.' The Associated Press, Reuters, Deutsche Welle, CNN, BBC, and TV5Monde all reported sweeping Democratic wins, with historic firsts including Abdul el-Sayed becoming the first Muslim senator, Adam Hamilton becoming the first Democrat from Kansas, and a record number of women in the next Congress. Trump initially accepted the results, saying 'Democrats did a good job,' but by November 9 he was questioning election integrity after previously accepting results, as the BBC noted. Republicans blamed Trump personally; the WSJ ran 'How Trump Lost the Midterms,' and the BBC reported 'Trumpism was rejected.' The MAGA coalition was described as shattered, and the 2028 race was thrown into chaos, with Harry Enten calling the results 'extinction level' for the GOP. Latino voters were a decisive factor, snubbing Trump after his hardline immigration stance, as TV5Monde and AFP reported. Elon Musk's half-billion-dollar injection into Republican campaigns was noted as potentially costly given the defeat.

In the White House, Trump made a series of dramatic moves in response. He appointed hardliner Stephen Miller as chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles, a move that multiple outlets framed as Trump charting a course for conflict rather than compromise. He offered UFC CEO Dana White the White House press secretary role, which White reportedly declined, then said he was 'only kidding.' He ordered the Justice Department to investigate Democrats for 'threatening' people. He designated the Oval Office a national monument. He made the Oval Office a national monument. A federal judge ordered a 14-day delay on construction of his monumental arch, and a judge wanted a former US attorney to investigate whether the government misled her in the golf case. Two arrests occurred near the White House in separate incidents, one involving a man who said he heard voices telling him to kill Trump. The head of the DOJ civil division resigned, and two other DOJ officials walked out, including the US attorney who oversaw the 'grand conspiracy' probe. Democrats in their new congressional power immediately prepared an investigative blitz, as the AP and FT noted.

On the Iran front, the US military carried out new targeted strikes on Iran, including hitting Qeshm Island and disabling a cargo vessel in the Gulf of Oman while expanding a naval blockade to restrict Iranian land commerce. The US offered a $20 million reward for information on Iran's nuclear program. Yet Trump repeatedly said renewed war was 'highly unlikely' if talks progressed, and he was set to meet Qatar's prime minister as a war mediator. Iran defended a two-day proposal for peace talks after the US rejected conditions. Oil fell nearly 5% on Trump's restraint signal. The US asked Iraq to shut most Iran border crossings, and Iraq reached understandings to allow oil exports through Hormuz. Trump acknowledged the Iran war 'cost Republicans' in the midterms.

On Israel, Trump announced the US was cutting off military aid to Israel at year's end, saying 'they don't need it,' which shocked Israel's president. Trump said his 'great dislike' for Israel contributed to Republican losses. This was a historic shift in US-Israel relations, as CNN and BBC reported.

On Ukraine, Melania Trump hosted Russian and Ukrainian delegations at the White House, calling for a 'more enduring' ceasefire, while Trump touted a deal for 'all of Europe.' The Kremlin hoped the US election shakeup would not shift Trump's negotiations. Analysts saw the midterm results as offering hope on Ukraine aid and Russia scrutiny.

In the economy and markets, the Dow had its best post-midterm day in 44 years as Democrats took control. Global tech stocks had plunged earlier in the week on AI slowdown fears, but recovered. Crypto slid to two-month lows. Trump's $1.5 trillion defense budget was set to be blocked by Democrats. US inflation was expected to simmer down. A Russian diesel deal with the US faltered as US fuel supplies hit a 20-year low. China extended the US trade truce by two months. The US and China confirmed discussions on a historic Xi-Trump-Putin meeting at the APEC summit. South Korea said a $10 billion US nuclear project remittance requires a full feasibility review. The G7 gathered in Paris to assess the impact of Trump's midterm setback.

In tech and AI, Trump signaled openness to AI guardrails, calling risks 'manageable.' The US center for AI safety was reporting to the White House, raising independence concerns. Nvidia faced a spy scandal. The US opened a probe into Waymo vehicles over school bus safety violations. The FDA ordered new eye risk warnings for Ozempic and Zepbound. The US was found exposed to the flesh-eating screwworm years into the outbreak. In the Southwest, rare floods brought relief to reservoirs as Lake Powell rose 20 feet, while desert icons collapsed under rain. Washington and Colorado voters approved transgender athlete bans. The Supreme Court's John Roberts set the stage for publicly funded religious schools to reject children of same-sex couples. The US slapped more sanctions on Cambodia's alleged scam group affiliates. China's giant pandas made their public debut at a US zoo. Meghan Markle's father was arrested in the US over child sex abuse images. Bob Dylan met Pope Leo XIV in Vatican City. Dolly Parton's manager dropped a lawsuit against her nephew. The Pope said he was 'proud to be an American' after the elections and credited God and doctors with his cancer rebound. Jay Rockefeller, former West Virginia governor and senator, died at 89.
measurement.expected:
Congressional transition and Democratic power: It is almost certain that the new Democratic-led Congress will convene, elect new leadership in both chambers, and begin the process of launching investigations into the Trump administration, the DOJ, and major corporations. The AP, FT, and CNN all noted Democrats are readying an investigative blitz. Expect hearings, subpoenas, and committee fights within the first days of the new session. Trump's $1.5 trillion defense budget will face its first real block, as Bloomberg reported, and a spending fight will begin. Probable that the first major legislative clash will center on the defense budget and possibly on the data center permitting bill that already got a first crack in Congress.

Iran diplomacy and the Gulf: It is probable that the Qatar-mediated peace talks will continue, with Trump meeting the Qatari prime minister and both sides testing the two-day proposal. Trump has repeatedly said war is 'highly unlikely' if talks progress, but the US military has been expanding its blockade and striking. Expect a tense week of back-and-forth, with the possibility of another limited US strike if Iran hardliners reject concessions. The $20 million reward for nuclear program information signals the US still wants leverage. Possible that a framework deal or at least a formal pause in hostilities is announced, but unlikely that a full peace agreement is signed this week. The US asking Iraq to shut Iran border crossings and the Hormuz oil export understandings will be active workstreams.

Israel aid and US-Israel relations: It is probable that the announcement to cut off Israel military aid at year's end will trigger a fierce congressional debate, with Democrats likely to push for a stopgap or conditions and Republicans (now in the minority) scrambling to protect the relationship. Trump's admission that his 'great dislike' for Israel cost Republicans will be a flashpoint. Possible that a stopgap funding package is negotiated to avoid an abrupt cutoff. Unlikely that the relationship fully normalizes or that a formal break is declared this week.

White House personnel and internal politics: It is almost certain that Stephen Miller will be fully installed as chief of staff and will begin reshaping the administration's priorities, pushing a harder line on immigration and domestic policy. The Dana White press secretary saga will either produce a follow-up or be quietly dropped. Expect more DOJ resignations or firings as the civil division head's departure creates a vacuum. Trump's questioning of election integrity, even after accepting results, will keep the narrative alive and fuel Republican infighting. Possible that Vance or another figure makes a public statement that further distances the VP from the president's Iran war stance.

Markets and economy: It is probable that the inflation data release will be closely watched, with Bloomberg noting inflation is set to simmer down. Tech stocks will try to recover from the AI-driven swoon, but the 'perp futures' risk and Nvidia spy scandal will keep volatility high. Crypto will likely remain range-bound near two-month lows until a clear policy signal from the new Democratic Congress. The Russian diesel deal and the China trade truce extension will be monitored. Possible that the G7 outcomes from Paris produce a joint statement on US tech reliance and trade. The $10 billion South Korea nuclear project feasibility review will be a slower-moving item.

Ukraine and Europe: It is possible that follow-up to Melania's hosting of Russian and Ukrainian delegations produces a more concrete ceasefire framework or at least a joint statement. Trump's reference to a deal for 'all of Europe' suggests he is packaging Ukraine into a broader settlement. The Kremlin's hope that the US shakeup won't shift negotiations will be tested. G7 allies in Paris will be assessing what the midterm setback means for transatlantic coordination. Possible that a modest additional aid package or conditional support is announced, but unlikely that a full peace deal is signed.

AI and tech regulation: It is possible that the first concrete moves toward AI guardrails appear, given Trump's openness signal and the independence concerns at the US center for AI safety. The Waymo probe and the FDA Ozempic/Zepbound eye warnings will generate consumer and industry headlines. The Nvidia spy scandal may spawn a congressional inquiry given the new Democratic majority. Unlikely that a sweeping AI bill is passed this week, but possible that a committee hearing is scheduled.

Immigration and domestic policy: It is probable that Trump's admission that deportation was 'too tough' leads to a softening in rhetoric, though Miller's appointment as chief of staff suggests the machinery will stay hard. The scuttled Iranian deportation flight and the hopeful migrants bound for the US will keep the border in the news. The trans athlete bans in Washington and Colorado will generate legal challenges. The screwworm outbreak will continue to be a public health story. The Oval Office national monument designation and the arch construction delay will remain active legal and political issues.

Less likely surprises: A second White House arrest or security incident at the Oval Office; a surprise Trump-Xi-Putin meeting announcement before the APEC summit; a major FDA drug approval or recall that dominates headlines; a state-level ballot measure result (abortion, taxes, foie gras) that sparks a national legal fight; the Mississippi Senate race finally being called and shifting the Senate math; a surprise Supreme Court ruling on the religious schools case.

Things I would not bet on: A full US-Iran peace deal signed this week; a formal US-Israel diplomatic break or a new US military ground deployment in the Middle East; a US recession declaration or a 500-point stock market crash; a second impeachment inquiry reaching a formal vote; a US presidential resignation or health emergency; a major natural disaster (hurricane, earthquake) hitting the continental US in this one-week window; a formal US withdrawal from NATO or a new major trade war with China beyond the existing truce.

delta.motion: The single most dramatic shift between the two photographs is the transformation of the midterm election from a looming, chaotic, heavily contested event into a settled, sweeping Democratic victory that has restructured the entire political landscape. On November 1, the story was about Trump's threats, the Alaska ballot fight, the California mail-ballot dispute, the Michigan 9/11 rhetoric, the telerallies, the AI chatbot disinformation, and the storm set to hit on Election Day. By November 9, all of that pre-election turbulence has vanished from the news cycle, replaced by the aftermath: Democrats flipping both chambers in what multiple outlets called a blue tsunami, historic firsts in the Senate, the MAGA coalition described as shattered, and the 2028 race thrown into chaos. The pre-election legal maneuvering that dominated the first photo — the WSJ lawsuit, the Alaska criminal probe, the specific ballot challenges — has largely receded, though the arch construction delay and the golf-case investigation persist in a slightly different form. What has grown enormously is the White House's reactive, almost performative response to the loss: the appointment of Stephen Miller as chief of staff, the designation of the Oval Office as a national monument, the offer of the press secretary role to Dana White, the DOJ order to investigate Democrats, the resignation of the DOJ civil division head, and the two arrests near the White House. None of these existed in the first photo. The Iran war has continued and evolved: the first photo showed threats of strikes and the $47 billion cost, while the second photo shows actual strikes on Qeshm Island, a disabled cargo vessel, a $20 million nuclear reward, a naval blockade expansion, and simultaneously diplomatic overtures through Qatar. The war is still active but now has a diplomatic track running alongside it, and Trump himself has acknowledged it cost Republicans the midterms. A major new theme has appeared that was barely present in the first photo: the US cutting off military aid to Israel, which Trump framed as partly caused by his great dislike for the country, and the Melania-hosted Ukraine-Russia delegation at the White House. The Bolsonaro drama, which was a prominent sidebar in the first photo, has largely faded from the second. The Cuba UN shouting match has also receded. On the economic side, the first photo showed pre-election jitters, the Fed holding rates, Alphabet's stock drop, and Boeing's stumble. The second photo shows the Dow having its best post-midterm day in 44 years, global tech stocks plunging on AI slowdown fears and then recovering, crypto at two-month lows, and the $1.5 trillion defense budget set to be blocked. The lighter cultural items from the first photo — the Nebraska soccer player, the necktie fashion piece, Dolores Huerta's death, Hayden Panettiere's death — have given way to a new set of cultural stories: the Pope's cancer rebound and his meeting with Bob Dylan, Meghan Markle's father's arrest, the pandas at a US zoo, Dolly Parton's manager dropping a lawsuit, and Jay Rockefeller's death. The overall motion is from anticipation and pre-election chaos to a settled but deeply consequential political realignment, with the executive branch reacting in ways that are more erratic and symbolic than the measured legal battles of the first week.
delta.wind: The expectation was broadly in the right direction but underestimated the scale of the Democratic victory. We expected a close, contested election with legal disputes in Alaska, California, and Michigan, and Trump questioning the results. That did happen, but the result was more of a landslide than a photo finish. We said the outcome would be close enough in two or three races to trigger disputes, but the blue tsunami was sweeping enough that the disputes are secondary to the overall shift in power. We were correct that Trump would publicly question the results, and he did, though he initially accepted them before reversing. We were right that at least one state would see challenges, but the challenges are less central than the broader Democratic consolidation. On Iran, we were substantially correct. We expected at least one limited strike, and the US hit Qeshm Island and a cargo vessel. We expected a short, intense exchange rather than a full ground war, and that is what happened. We expected Pakistan-mediated talks, but Qatar emerged as the more prominent mediator, with Trump set to meet Qatar's prime minister. We were right that a formal ceasefire was unlikely within the window. We did not anticipate the $20 million nuclear reward, the Iraq border crossing shutdown, or the oil price drop on Trump's restraint signal. On the Bolsonaro situation, we expected him to hold public appearances and for Brazil to issue diplomatic protests, but the story has largely faded from the US news cycle by the second photo. This suggests the Bolsonaro drama, while newsworthy in week one, did not sustain momentum. On the economy, we were right that markets would react sharply and that the Democratic takeover would hit defense and energy stocks, with the $1.5 trillion defense budget now set to be blocked. We did not anticipate the global tech stock plunge on AI slowdown fears, the crypto slide, the Russian diesel deal faltering, or the G7 gathering in Paris. On legal battles, we were right about the arch facing a construction delay and the golf-case investigation producing a public filing. We did not anticipate the Oval Office being designated a national monument, the Stephen Miller appointment, the Dana White offer, or the DOJ civil division head's resignation. These are new, reactive moves that the first photo's legal landscape did not foreshadow. On foreign policy, we expected another US-Cuba spat, but it did not materialize prominently. We expected US-Russia talks to produce a framework, and the Melania-hosted delegation and Trump's Europe deal talk are in that direction, though less formal than we anticipated. The biggest miss was Israel: we did not expect the US to cut off military aid to Israel at year's end, a historic shift that was barely a footnote in the first photo. We also did not anticipate the Xi-Trump-Putin APEC meeting discussions or the China trade truce extension. Among the surprises we listed, the Nvidia spy scandal and the Waymo probe fit the pattern of a major corporate or tech announcement. The two arrests near the White House and the Pope's cancer rebound were not in our surprise list. Overall, the expectation framework captured the major structural forces — the election, Iran, the legal battles, the market reaction — but underestimated the speed and scale of the Democratic victory, overestimated the persistence of the Bolsonaro and Cuba stories, and did not anticipate the White House's more symbolic, almost theatrical post-election moves or the Israel aid cut.
delta.driver: The central force pushing the United States from the first photograph to the second is the election result itself and the political realignment it has triggered. A bruised, cost-of-living-angry electorate, with Latino voters decisively snubbing Trump after his hardline immigration stance, delivered Democrats a rare dual-chamber victory that shattered the MAGA coalition and handed Congress a new investigative and legislative agenda. Trump, facing a weakened position, has responded not with compromise but with a series of symbolic and confrontational moves — the Miller appointment, the Oval Office monument, the DOJ investigation of Democrats, the Dana White stunt — that read as a man consolidating his inner circle and asserting executive prerogative even as his institutional leverage shrinks. The Iran war, which Trump himself acknowledged cost Republicans the midterms, continues as both a military and diplomatic track, giving him a post-election freedom of action in the Gulf while the new Congress looms with budget and oversight power. The Israel aid cut, the Ukraine-Russia White House meeting, and the APEC summit discussions all point to a foreign policy in rapid recalibration, partly driven by the need to show the new Congress that the executive is delivering results on the world stage. Beneath all of this is a deeper current: the shift from a Trump administration that could act with relative impunity in a divided or friendly Congress to one that must now fight for every initiative in a hostile legislature, and the corresponding shift in the White House from policy execution to political performance and symbolic assertion of power.

crystal.reasoning:
Starting from the present: the single most consequential fact is that Democrats now control both chambers of Congress after a sweeping 'blue tsunami,' and Trump has responded not with compromise but with a cascade of symbolic, confrontational, and almost theatrical moves — Miller as chief of staff, the Oval Office as a national monument, the Dana White press secretary offer, the DOJ ordered to investigate Democrats, the civil division head resigning. The motion tells me this is not a man negotiating from strength; it is a man performing power while his institutional leverage shrinks. The wind tells me I have consistently underestimated the scale and speed of his reactive, performative moves (I missed the Oval Office monument, the Miller appointment, the Dana White stunt, the Israel aid cut, the Xi-Trump-Putin APEC discussions) while overestimating the persistence of secondary stories (Bolsonaro, Cuba). So for next week, I weight heavily the continuation of Trump's symbolic escalation and the immediate Democratic congressional offensive, and I discount the likelihood that smaller threads (pandas, Dolly Parton, Bob Dylan-Pope) will reappear.

Extending each theme along its motion: The Democratic investigative blitz is now in its first 72 hours of real power. Committees will be staffed, subpoenas drafted, hearings scheduled. The $1.5 trillion defense budget is set to be blocked, which means a legislative fight begins this week. The Iran dual track — strikes on Qeshm, the naval blockade, the $20 million nuclear reward, the Qatar mediation, the Iraq border crossings — is in a holding pattern where both sides are testing limits without committing to a full war. The Israel aid cut is a bomb that has been announced but not yet detonated in its full diplomatic consequences. The Ukraine deal narrative, signaled by the Melania-hosted delegations and Trump's 'all of Europe' framing, is in the announcement phase. The markets are in a post-midterm rally that will face its first real test when the budget fight and defense spending cuts hit the numbers.

Correcting for the wind: I have been too conservative on Trump's personal, almost impulsive governance style. I have been too dismissive of the speed at which a new Congress acts. I have been too focused on the Iran war as a single escalating arc when it is actually two parallel tracks that can resolve independently. I have been too slow to see the Israel relationship shifting from a given to a negotiation. I have also been too quick to assume that secondary stories (Bolsonaro, Cuba) will persist; they fade fast. For next week, I therefore: (1) expect at least one more dramatic Trump symbolic or confrontational move that I cannot name in advance; (2) expect the Democratic Congress to announce at least two major investigation launches or committee hearings; (3) expect the Iran situation to see one more limited military action AND one more diplomatic step, not a full war or a full ceasefire; (4) expect the Israel aid cut to generate a visible diplomatic reaction from Jerusalem and possibly a partial walk-back or clarification from Trump; (5) expect the Ukraine deal to move from 'we are talking' to 'here is a framework'; (6) expect the markets to have one more volatile day on the defense budget or a tech/AI headline; (7) expect the arch and golf-case legal battles to produce at least one more court filing or ruling.

What I would not bet on: a full ground invasion of Iran, a second impeachment vote in this window (too early, though it will be discussed), a government shutdown (Democrats would fight it but likely not force it in week one), a major natural disaster, a banking or crypto crisis, Trump resigning, a full Ukraine ceasefire signed, the Pope story dominating US coverage, or a second wave of the Oval Office monument controversy. I would also not bet on the APEC summit producing a concrete three-way meeting announcement within this exact week, though the discussions will be reported.

crystal.eli5:
Imagine your school just had a big election, and the team you supported won by a landslide. Now the new student council gets to start checking the old council's homework, asking for receipts, and deciding how the school budget gets spent. That is basically what is happening in Washington this week. The Democrats just took control of both the House and the Senate, and they are immediately starting to dig into what the White House and the Justice Department have been doing. They are also going to fight over a huge defense spending bill that Trump wants to pass.

At the same time, President Trump is not sitting still. He has been making a bunch of big, dramatic announcements — like making the Oval Office a 'national monument' or offering a job to a UFC boss. He is doing this because he lost the election and wants to show he is still in charge. Think of it like a kid who lost a board game and keeps making new house rules to stay ahead. It is not necessarily fair, but it is what he is doing.

Out in the world, the US and Iran are still fighting a bit — small strikes here and there — but they are also trying to talk through a mediator in Qatar. It is like two kids in a playground who are still throwing rocks but also trying to work out a truce. The US also told Israel it is cutting off some military help, which is a big deal because the US has been Israel's biggest supporter for a long time. Israel is not happy about it.

On the Ukraine front, there is hope that a deal might actually come together. The First Lady hosted Russian and Ukrainian delegations at the White House, which is a sign that people are trying to get a ceasefire or at least a framework for peace. It is not signed yet, but it is moving in the right direction.

So the short version: a lot of political fighting at home, some continued tension with Iran, a historic shift in the US-Israel relationship, and a small ray of hope on Ukraine. It is a busy, dramatic week, and there will probably be at least one or two more surprises that nobody saw coming.

At the same time, President Trump is not sitting still. He has been making a bunch of big, dramatic announcements — like making the Oval Office a 'national monument' or offering a job to a UFC boss. He is doing this because he lost the election and wants to show he is still in charge. Think of it like a kid who lost a board game and keeps making new house rules to stay ahead. It is not necessarily fair, but it is what he is doing.

Out in the world, the US and Iran are still fighting a bit — small strikes here and there — but they are also trying to talk through a mediator in Qatar. It is like two kids in a playground who are still throwing rocks but also trying to work out a truce. The US also told Israel it is cutting off some military help, which is a big deal because the US has been Israel's biggest supporter for a long time. Israel is not happy about it.

On the Ukraine front, there is hope that a deal might actually come together. The First Lady hosted Russian and Ukrainian delegations at the White House, which is a sign that people are trying to get a ceasefire or at least a framework for peace. It is not signed yet, but it is moving in the right direction.

So the short version: a lot of political fighting at home, some continued tension with Iran, a historic shift in the US-Israel relationship, and a small ray of hope on Ukraine. It is a busy, dramatic week, and there will probably be at least one or two more surprises that nobody saw coming.

THE WAR AND STRIKES: The dominant story this week was a brutal escalation of mutual strikes between Russia and Ukraine, timed just days before US-brokered peace talks were to begin. Russia launched what multiple sources called 'massive' overnight strikes on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, power substations, bridges, and civilian centers. Kyiv lost power to hundreds of thousands of residents, and the death toll from a single strike on an aid center in Zaporizhzhia region climbed to between 31 and 53 depending on the source and the day. Russia also hit a hospital, a hospice, and a school used as an aid center, and in a particularly grim episode, targeted emergency crews already responding to a bombing (a so-called double-tap strike). Zelensky and the Kyiv mayor publicly traded blame over the city's darkness. On the ground, the Wall Street Journal reported that in ten months of fighting Russia gained only 46 square miles, and Bloomberg noted that hacked records suggest around 400,000 Russian soldiers have been killed, with TV5Monde reporting 350 conscripts killed in a single period. Russia's land gains are dwindling. Ukraine, meanwhile, intensified its campaign against Russian oil refineries, hitting the Ryazan plant, the Saratov refinery, the Yanos refinery, and what NASA satellite imagery confirmed as a major oil hub on fire. Kyiv hit its sixth Russian oil plant in a single week, and Zelensky confirmed the campaign would continue. (Supporting headlines: Reuters Nov 7 'Russia pounds power facilities around Kyiv'; AFP Nov 8 'Russian strikes cut power to hundreds of thousands'; CNN Nov 8 'Putin appears set on wrecking Ukraine's economy'; Bloomberg Nov 6 'Kyiv Hits Sixth Russian Oil Plant in a Week'; BBC Nov 3 'Russian bombing kills 31 at aid centre'; Al Jazeera Nov 9 'At least four killed as Russia and Ukraine trade strikes overnight'; WSJ Nov 7 'Ten Months of War to Gain 46 Square Miles'.)

PEACE TALKS AND DIPLOMACY: The second major thread was the rapid build-up toward US-led trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi, expected to begin around November 10. Trump met Putin's envoy Kirill Dmitriev at the White House and described the emerging framework as a 'big, beautiful' deal for all of Europe. Melania Trump positioned herself as an 'exclusive intermediary,' hosting both Russian and Ukrainian delegations at the White House to tout a local ceasefire. Russia upgraded its delegation for the talks, and European security agencies joined in an effort to shape the security-guarantee language. Trump said he expects to meet both Xi and Putin at the APEC summit in China, and China confirmed discussions are underway for that historic trilateral meeting. Iran's security chief met Putin and delivered a message from Khamenei, and a rocket-launcher deal deepened the Russia-Iran military tie. Turkey's Erdogan said he wants to discuss ending the war with Putin after talks with Zelensky. The Kremlin, however, accused Europe of struggling to decide who will speak for it at future security talks, and the EU's Kallas said Russia is 'pretending' to negotiate while 'bombing civilians.' MEDIA AND INFORMATION WAR: Novaya Gazeta, Russia's most prominent independent newspaper, officially closed its editorial office after three decades, citing official pressure. The Russian military began using deepfake videos to claim battlefield success. A covert Russian network was found to have exploited French riots on social media, according to an EU report. Pro-Russian hackers targeted Italy's foreign minister, and Estonia accused Russia of state-sponsored terrorism over a series of hybrid attacks. Both Russia and Ukraine reported that their emergency alert apps were hacked, with fake nuclear warnings sent to citizens in both countries. Rosstat, Russia's statistics agency, struggled to restore systems after a major cyberattack, and Belarusian hackers claimed to have obtained data on Russian military losses. crystal.eli5:
Next week, the big story is a meeting in Abu Dhabi where the US, Russia, and Ukraine sit down to talk about ending the war. President Trump is very excited about it and calls it a 'big beautiful deal,' and his wife Melania is trying to be a peacemaker too. But Russia and Ukraine are still bombing each other hard while they talk, so don't expect them to shake hands and sign a paper. Think of it like two kids arguing in a classroom while the teacher tries to get them to make up: they'll talk, they'll say some nice things, but they probably won't fully solve their problem yet.

At the same time, Russia is running out of gas, literally. Ukraine has been bombing Russian oil refineries nonstop, and now regular people in Russian cities can't find enough petrol or diesel to drive their cars or heat their homes. It's like if your local gas station ran out of fuel for the third week in a row. The Russian government is trying to hide how bad it is, but the cracks are showing: they're cutting pay for soldiers' families, and the economy is barely growing.

There's also a lot of drama in the information world. Russia just shut down its last big independent newspaper, and the military is making fake videos that look real to show off battlefield wins. Both Russia and Ukraine had their phone alert apps hacked, so people got fake warnings that a nuclear bomb was coming. It's like if your school's emergency alert system started going off for no reason, and then someone made a fake video of the principal saying the school was on fire. Everyone gets confused and a little scared.

And in a smaller but weird story, a court in Switzerland said Russia gets to play in the junior ice hockey championship, and now Canada, Finland, and several other countries are threatening to boycott the whole tournament. Putin is mad and says the countries that don't want Russia to play are 'violating democratic bodies,' which is like a kid in a playground saying the other kids are breaking the rules of the game just because they don't want him to play.

emoji_reasons: Russia's week was defined by massive airstrikes on Ukraine's energy grid and cities, with dozens killed, hundreds of thousands left without power, and a pattern of double-tap strikes on emergency crews, making the bombing the single most consequential event.

The rapid build-up to US-brokered trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi, Melania Trump's intermediary role, the Trump-Dmitriev meeting, and the planned Trump-Xi-Putin summit made peace diplomacy the week's central diplomatic thread, even as both sides kept striking.

Novaya Gazeta's closure after three decades, the deepfake battlefield videos, the hacked emergency apps in both countries, the EU report on Russian social-media manipulation of French riots, and the cyberattack on Rosstat together made the information and media war a defining undercurrent of the week.

measurement.happened:
The single dominant story of the week in China was the Nvidia spy scandal. Jensen Huang was reported to have had a romantic affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman the US believes was a Chinese spy who spent years in Nvidia's orbit and pitched AI chip deals to investors. Nvidia launched an internal investigation, Huang admitted the affair, and the company's shares fell. China's Foreign Ministry called the whole episode baseless smears and slander, while Trump publicly backed Huang. Key Republican lawmakers demanded a briefing from Huang over the Chinese spy allegations, and the US Treasury and Commerce raised compliance concerns. Bloomberg ran a piece titled Everything Jensen Huang Said About China Is Out the Window, and multiple outlets noted that Nvidia ordered its data-center clients to reduce China exposure. Chinese media and the public were visibly angry at what they saw as a US smear campaign. This story touched every corner of the US-China tech relationship and will likely shape chip policy and trade talks for months. (Headlines: Reuters, AP, AFP, BBC, CNN, Deutsche Welle, TV5Monde, Bloomberg, WSJ, FT, CNBC, Al Jazeera.)

The second major theme was the extension of the US-China trade truce and related measures. China extended the suspension of new rare earth export controls until January, extended the pause on US tariffs and trade curbs by two months, extended the suspension of port fees on US-linked ships, and extended the sanctions suspension on South Korea's Hanwha Ocean by two months. The US, meanwhile, urged China to immediately meet its rare earths and agriculture commitments under the Busan deal, and Treasury Secretary Bessent and Trade Representative Greer raised compliance concerns. China said US farm purchases hinge on a tariff-cut deal, and it kept anti-dumping and anti-subsidy tariffs on US n-propanol imports for five more years. The US also targeted China-based suppliers in its escalation against Cuba. The overall tone was one of cautious continuation rather than a new breakthrough. (Headlines: Reuters, Bloomberg, FT, CNBC, Al Jazeera, Deutsche Welle.)

China's domestic economy and markets were a third major theme. Producer inflation (PPI) hit its highest level in over four years at 5.7 percent, while consumer inflation (CPI) moderated. The National Team, China's state-linked trading entities, ramped up ETF buying to a record high to stabilize the stock market. Beijing halted new IPO listings to protect the market from the AI-driven selloff, and the State Council called for stronger stock market stability. The central bank tweaked forex reserve rules and Chinese banks boosted dollar deposit rates to smooth the yuan's rally. The NDRC flagged weak domestic demand as a key challenge. China's quants swung to losses after the October tech selloff, a top-rated firm faced sudden distress testing the rating crackdown, and bad-debt collectors are chasing roughly 100 million defaulters. China's car exports are forecast to slow from a supercharged pace, and Siemens Healthineers and BMW both reported weaker results partly due to China weakness. On the positive side, China's Q3 emissions posted the biggest drop since the pandemic, China is set to lead the world in energy investment in 2026, and China started marketing green bonds for debut sales in Canada. (Headlines: Reuters, Bloomberg, WSJ, FT, CNBC, Deutsche Welle, TV5Monde.)

Diplomacy and the upcoming APEC summit formed a fourth theme. Trump said he expects to meet Xi and Putin at the China APEC summit, and China confirmed discussions are underway on a historic three-way meeting. The US, Russia, and China are all discussing logistics. Japan is working to shield its leader Takaichi from any snub by Xi at the summit. Senior Chinese and North Korean officials met in Beijing to urge closer ties. China and Gabon elevated their relationship with pledges on mining and security. China warned the Philippines to be cautious over the South China Sea. Taiwan detained a Communist Party leader over alleged Chinese sponsorship in its mayoral election, and also shut its Papua New Guinea office and ended LNG buying, citing Chinese pressure. China disputed reports of an artillery shell found in PNG. Italy's prosecutors targeted a China-linked network accused of tracking a dissident. (Headlines: Reuters, AP, Bloomberg, FT, CNBC, Al Jazeera, Deutsche Welle.)

Technology and AI were a fifth theme. Apple's Intelligence AI service registered with China's regulator for use on tablets and laptops, marking the arrival of Apple AI tools in China after a two-year delay. China blocked SoftBank's 5.4-billion-dollar acquisition of ABB's robotics division, flexing control over AI tech, and SoftBank and ABB are now exploring a China carve-out to salvage the deal. China's top flash memory chipmaker is targeting more homegrown tools for a new factory. China's Moonshot AI lab turned to Europe for Nvidia Blackwell chip access amid US-China curbs. Beijing sought to bolster AI shares, and the US-China AI arms race was described as escalating. China's critical minerals dominance left the UK dangerously exposed, MPs warned, and China expanded its overseas mining stakes. The EU validated JD.com's acquisition of the second-largest stake in Fnac Darty. (Headlines: Reuters, Bloomberg, WSJ, FT, CNBC, Deutsche Welle, TV5Monde, AFP.)

Political and institutional moves formed a sixth theme. China shifted several former provincial leaders to the legislature in what was described as soft retirement. Former Politburo member Ma Xingrui was charged with taking bribes. Xi tapped a military hatchet man to rebuild China's army command. China raised its delegate count to 2,360 for the 2027 Party Congress. China passed a cross-border corruption law expanding the anti-graft drive, and adopted a law on Antarctic activities and environmental protection. In Macau, an ex-lawmaker was sentenced to jail in the territory's first national security trial. A pastor at a Beijing underground church was arrested. The Financial Times ran a piece on the perils of Xi Jinping's purge. (Headlines: Reuters, AP, Bloomberg, FT, BBC.)

Space and science were a smaller but notable theme. A Pakistani astronaut will join China's Shenzhou-24 mission and become the first foreigner on China's space station. China's swarm strategy for the space race was profiled. (Headlines: Reuters, AP, Al Jazeera, FT.)

Culture, sports, and society rounded out the week. Kylian Mbappe's Mao comments led to China contacting Real Madrid and LaLiga, and Chinese state TV pulled La Liga matches. Mone Chiba won the Cup of China in figure skating. Chinese giant pandas made their public debut at an Atlanta zoo. Chinese motorcycles are conquering Europe. A former elementary school teacher became the newest paper billionaire in China. China's marriage rate in the third quarter tumbled to an 18-year low. Hyrox fitness events took off in China. Chinese e-bikes boomed as fuel prices rose. A building fire in Taiyuan killed 14. Tropical Storm Champi battered Taiwan and Japan before nearing China. Two Uyghur men in Thailand pleaded not to be sent back to China. An Astellas employee imprisoned in China is to be released in December. (Headlines: Reuters, AP, AFP, BBC, CNBC, Al Jazeera, Deutsche Welle, TV5Monde.)

delta.motion: Between the two photographs, the Nvidia spy scandal grew from a secondary story into the single dominant narrative of the week. In the first photograph it was a reported suspicion, a denial from Beijing, and Nvidia's claim that the matter was 'investigated and debunked.' Eight days later, Jensen Huang had admitted a romantic affair with a Chinese businesswoman the US believes was a spy, Nvidia had launched an internal investigation, its shares had fallen, US lawmakers were demanding briefings, and Treasury and Commerce had raised formal compliance concerns. The story accelerated from rumor to confirmed scandal at a very fast pace, touching chip policy, trade talks, and the broader US-China AI rivalry all at once. The Mbappé-Mao cultural storm shrank sharply. It was the loudest, most-covered item in the first photograph, spanning at least ten outlets and a dozen headlines. By the second photograph it was one entry in a culture-and-sports roundup alongside a figure-skating trophy, a panda debut in Atlanta, and a motorcycle trend. The Sanrio-Hello Kitty episode, which had drawn a second wave of commentary in the first week, vanished entirely. The US-China trade lane shifted in character: the first photograph showed a flurry of new restrictions (FCC lab ban, biotech limits, telecom phone-number ban, truck-trailer tariffs) punctuated by a small thaw in wheat. The second photograph shows the opposite motion, a broad extension of the existing truce, with rare-earth export controls paused until January, tariff suspensions extended by two months, port-fee suspensions continued, and Hanwha Ocean sanctions held. The tone moved from new friction to cautious continuation, with both sides pressing on compliance rather than adding new measures. The economic picture became more complex rather than simply worse. The first photograph showed a contracting PMI and a wall of weak earnings from European and Japanese automakers. The second photograph revealed producer inflation at 5.7 percent, the highest in over four years, even as consumer inflation moderated. The government's response shifted from passive observation to active intervention: the National Team ramped ETF buying to a record, Beijing halted new IPO listings, the State Council called for stronger market stability, and the central bank tweaked forex-reserve rules. The party-politics thread continued but changed shape. The first photograph featured the plenum, 33 expulsions, and the Zhang Shengmin elevation. The second photograph shows the aftermath playing out in specific institutional moves: Ma Xingrui charged with bribery, a military hatchet man tapped to rebuild army command, a cross-border corruption law passed, the 2027 Party Congress delegate count raised to 2,360, and several former provincial leaders shifted to the legislature in soft retirement. The APEC summit, barely a footnote in the first photograph (an Australian PM visit was mentioned), grew into a major diplomatic event, with Trump saying he expects to meet Xi and Putin and all three sides discussing logistics for what could be a historic three-way meeting. New themes appeared that were absent or minor in the first photograph: Apple's Intelligence AI service registering with China's regulator after a two-year delay, China blocking SoftBank's 5.4-billion-dollar acquisition of ABB's robotics division, a Pakistani astronaut set to become the first foreigner on China's space station, a cross-border corruption law, an Antarctic activities law, a Macau national-security trial, China's green-bond debut in Canada, and the marriage rate falling to an 18-year low. In short, the motion from one photograph to the next is driven by a single underlying tension: China trying to hold together a stable, confident, and institutionally consolidated front while the US presses on the exact technology (AI chips) that is central to its growth strategy, and the domestic economy sends mixed signals that demand active management rather than passive stimulus.

Next week, China is hosting a big international meeting called APEC, where the leaders of the US, China, and Russia might all sit at the same table for the first time in a while. Think of it like a school assembly where three loud kids who keep arguing in the hallway are finally put in the same room. Everyone will take photos, say nice things, and probably agree to keep talking. Nobody expects a perfect solution, but everyone wants to look like they're getting along.

At the same time, the big drama about the boss of Nvidia (the company that makes the computer chips for AI) and a Chinese woman who might have been a spy is still going. Next week, the boss has to go in front of lawmakers and explain what happened. It's like a student who was caught talking to a new kid in class, and now the principal wants to know if the new kid was actually a spy from the rival school. The whole thing is making both the US and China a little angry and a little nervous about who gets to build the smartest computers.

Back home in China, the economy is sending mixed signals. Factory prices went up a lot (which is usually a good thing, but it also means things are getting more expensive), while regular people are still not spending as much as they used to. The government is trying to keep the stock market from dropping by buying shares themselves, kind of like a parent quietly putting money in their kid's piggy bank so it doesn't look empty. They're not giving everyone a big bonus, but they're trying to make sure the piggy bank doesn't run out. There's also a lot of behind-the-scenes shuffling in the government, with some officials getting promoted, some getting retired, and a few getting in trouble for taking bribes. It's a lot like the student council at the end of the year, where some kids stay on and some get new jobs.

measurement.happened:
This week in DR Congo was dominated by a terrifying convergence of two crises: a massive Ebola outbreak and renewed armed violence in the east, compounded by a web of mining disputes and political maneuvering.

Ebola was the single biggest story. The outbreak has now killed more than 5,300 people, with a fatality rate topping 50 percent according to Bloomberg. The World Health Organization gave the green light to clinical trials of two new Ebola vaccines, and Médecins Sans Frontières issued an urgent appeal to widen access to the existing Ervebo vaccine. The human toll was made painfully visible when a British doctor who tested positive in Congo was evacuated to London for treatment, and Ebola survivors were filmed comforting sick children in isolation wards. The outbreak also intersected with the security crisis: IS-linked Islamist militants raided a village in North Kivu, killing at least 33 people and forcing Ebola patients to flee their treatment facilities, a scene captured in a TV5Monde video report. A cholera epidemic running in parallel has already claimed 1,800 lives since the start of the year, according to the WHO, and an anthrax outbreak that killed hippos in Virunga National Park has prompted authorities to warn of possible transmission to humans. The health system is stretched to breaking point, with overcrowded classrooms and food insecurity making the population more vulnerable.

In the security sphere, the 33-killing village attack by IS-linked militants (reported by AP, Al Jazeera, Reuters, and TV5Monde) was the most violent single event of the week. Residents of Uvira in South Kivu told TV5Monde they live in a state of 'psychose' and fear a return of full-scale war. Armed groups are also taxing beer transporters on the roads, squeezing local commerce. The broader context includes ongoing US sanctions on Rwanda tied to the Congo war, as discussed in a BBC broadcast, and the DRC-Rwanda tension that colored the Francophonie organization's leadership election.

On the minerals and mining front, a busy week of disputes unfolded. The Congo government opened a fraud inquiry after seizing copper and cobalt shipments it deemed illegally mined. Residents filed a lawsuit against a Chinese copper mine over alleged pollution. Kinshasa told China's Huayou Cobalt that its unit must pay six million dollars in compensation despite a project halt. The country also said the US minerals deal should be judged by actual projects on the ground rather than signed agreements, signaling a more pragmatic posture. Bloomberg reported that Trafigura-led creditors took a 70 percent loss on a Congolese miner's debt, and the government is now seeking twelve billion dollars in investor money to fix chronic power shortages. The Lobito Corridor, a major port-to-port logistics project, remains largely unknown to the communities it is supposed to serve, according to a TV5Monde video.

Politically, the Senate definitively adopted a controversial referendum law, closing out a long parliamentary saga. The opposition C64 alliance was warned its leaders could be arrested for meeting with former president Joseph Kabila, a move that reads as a power play. The Francophonie election took place under the shadow of the DRC-Rwanda rivalry. The US and DRC signaled they would accelerate economic cooperation and investment, per a BBC broadcast in Kirundi.

A lighter note: a teenager from conflict-hit Congo made history at the Youth Olympics, competing with his father as coach, a small story of resilience amid the chaos.

What was a single-disease story in the first photograph has become a multi-disease health emergency: a cholera epidemic that has already killed 1,800 people this year now runs in parallel, and an anthrax outbreak in Virunga National Park has killed hippos and prompted warnings about human transmission. The health system is not just strained by Ebola; it is being hit from three directions at once.

Security violence shifted in character. In the first photograph, the military narrative was dominated by Kabila's FRN movement and the M23 conflict, with the US sanctions on Rwanda as the headline. In the second, the most violent single event is an IS-linked militant raid on a village in North Kivu that killed at least 33 people and forced Ebola patients to flee their treatment facilities. The ADF, which in the first photo was a background story about gold smuggling, has become the face of the violence. Kabila's FRN, which was a major standalone story, has receded in visibility; Kabila now appears more as a political target (the C64 opposition was warned its leaders could be arrested for meeting him) than as an active rebel commander on the ground. Uvira residents describe living in a state of 'psychose,' but no new FRN offensive has materialized in the coverage.

The mining and minerals sector grew from a couple of discrete stories into a dense cluster of legal, financial, and diplomatic disputes. The first photograph had the suspension of the artisanal mining agency head and a Gates-backed company complaining about China. The second shows a fraud inquiry after the government seized copper and cobalt shipments, a resident lawsuit against a Chinese copper mine over pollution, a demand that Huayou Cobalt pay six million dollars in compensation, the US minerals deal being reframed as something to be judged by actual projects rather than signed agreements, Trafigura-led creditors taking a 70 percent loss on a Congolese miner's debt, and the government seeking twelve billion dollars in investor money to fix chronic power shortages. The Lobito Corridor logistics project also surfaced, with communities it is supposed to serve saying they know little about it. The sector has gone from 'one agency head suspended' to a multi-front legal and financial confrontation.

The C64 opposition went from meeting in Rome and calling for dialogue to being warned its leaders could be arrested for meeting Kabila. The Francophonie leadership election appeared as a new arena where the DRC-Rwanda rivalry played out. The US and DRC signaled they would accelerate economic cooperation, a positive note that sat alongside the ongoing sanctions on Rwanda.

crystal.eli5:
Imagine a country where three different emergencies are happening at the same time, in the same hospitals, with the same doctors and nurses. That is DR Congo right now. Ebola has killed more than 5,300 people, but it is not the only disease: cholera has killed 1,800 people this year, and a germ that killed hippos in a national park is now being watched because it might jump to humans. All three diseases are fighting for the same small number of beds, the same small number of health workers, and the same community trust that is already shaky because armed groups keep attacking villages.

In the eastern part of the country, a group of fighters linked to the Islamic State has been the main source of violence. Last week they raided a village and killed 33 people, and some of the people who ran for help were Ebola patients leaving a treatment center. This is the kind of thing that makes the crises feel like one big mess instead of separate problems. The former president, Kabila, is still a big political figure, but he is more of a target the government is angry at than a general leading an army. The real killing is being done by the IS-linked fighters.

The economy is tangled up in all of this. The government seized some copper and cobalt that it thinks was mined illegally, and now there is a fraud investigation. A Chinese mining company is being sued by local residents over pollution. Another Chinese company is being told to pay six million dollars. A European group of lenders lost 70 percent of their money on a Congolese mining company. And the government is asking investors for twelve billion dollars to fix the power grid, which is a huge number. All of this is happening while the United States is sanctioning Rwanda's military but also telling Congo it wants to invest more money there. It is a lot of threads pulled in different directions at the same time.

Politically, the government has been winning. The Senate voted to make a controversial referendum law official, which closes that chapter. But the opposition group called C64 has been warned that its leaders could be arrested just for meeting with the former president. So next week, we might see either actual arrests or a very angry public speech from the opposition. The government is trying to look in control while the ground reality is getting more tangled.

The most important thing to watch is not any single story but the way the stories bump into each other. An ADF raid that also kicks up a cholera treatment center. A mining dispute that turns into a protest in a village already hit by Ebola. A new vaccine trial milestone that gets overshadowed by another village attack. The country is not dealing with three separate crises. It is dealing with one big knot, and next week the knot gets tighter.

A fraud inquiry, a pollution lawsuit, a six-million-dollar compensation demand against Huayou, a 70 percent creditor loss, and a twelve-billion-dollar power investment search made the minerals and mining economy the week's third major theme.

measurement.happened:
The dominant story of the week in Iran was the ongoing US-Iran war and the seismic political shock of the US midterm elections on November 4, which Democrats won in a sweep, with the Iran war widely blamed for the Republican rout. Trump himself acknowledged the war cost his party, and Vice President Vance openly repudiated it, saying 'everyone knows why we lost.' House Democrats immediately pledged to make ending the war their top priority, and a shutdown risk emerged as they considered ways to force a conclusion. This put Trump in a bind: he wanted to look tough but could no longer afford a costly escalation without Congressional support. He repeatedly said renewed strikes were 'highly unlikely' if talks showed progress, while still confirming that the US had carried out 'minor strikes' on Iran's Qeshm Island on November 3, hours before the vote, and that missiles had hit the island again on November 6. Rubio called the war 'necessary' to stop the nuclear threat but admitted it was 'not necessarily popular.' Hegseth defended the war from the Pentagon and waved off the expected impeachment push.

The Strait of Hormuz remained the theater of constant friction. Iran's IRGC struck two tankers and a tugboat on November 5, hit three more tankers on November 9 over 'US links,' and destroyed navigation aids overnight. Iran turned to what the Wall Street Journal called 'guerrilla tactics' to reassert its grip on the strait, while the US expanded its naval blockade and launched a new task force to restrict Iran's land-based arms supply routes through Iraq and other corridors. The US also asked Iraq to shut most Iran border crossings. Iran exempted India, China, Qatar, and Iraq from its Hormuz restrictions, signaling selective pressure. A Gulf tanker was attacked with one seafarer killed on November 6, and Iran-linked ships were seen hovering over subsea cables after threats.

Diplomacy ran in parallel but without a breakthrough. Qatar continued to mediate, with its prime minister meeting Trump on November 9 and the emir holding a call with Trump on November 6. Iran sent a nuclear proposal to the US via Qatar, and Bloomberg reported the two sides were 'edging closer to a deal' with the nuclear issue back in play. However, Rubio called Iran's demands 'outrageous' and saw no imminent breakthrough. Iran defended a two-day proposal for peace talks after the US rejected its conditions. Iran's chief negotiator said the US must act to prevent renewed war, and Khamenei empowered the talks while Trump said a deal 'could arrive.' The overall picture was one of cautious, slow movement rather than a cliff-edge deal.

On the economic front, the war's impact was severe. Iran's oil exports were near zero according to FGE. The US sanctioned Indian and Turkish firms and eight Canadian money-services companies for aiding Iran. The US offered a $20 million reward for information on Iran's nuclear program, despite Trump's earlier claims of having 'obliterated' it. Oil prices swung wildly, ultimately falling more than 5 percent in a single day on November 8 and recording the biggest weekly decline since 2020, dipping below $90 a barrel. The Bank of England raised rates for the first time since the war began, warning inflation would near 5 percent. Emirates' profit plunged, the IEA warned the war threatened a record annual drop in global LNG supply, and the Philippines' economic slump worsened. A little-known Chinese bank was found at the center of Iranian and Russian money flows.

Domestically, Iran tightened its grip. Three men were executed for 'armed unrest' during the January protests, and a Baluch militant was hanged for an armed attack on a police station. The authorities hardened domestic security controls amid US strike threats, cracked down on clerics, and pressured college students. The IRGC announced it was building underground sites for weapons production and storage, and satellite images showed major construction near missile bases. Iran's army declared itself 'stronger' than at the start of the war, and the country lifted its self-imposed limit on missile ranges. The son of Iran's ousted Shah received the 'Freedom Prize' in Frankfurt, sparking controversy. A deportation flight of Iranians from the US was scuttled at the last minute after the Trump administration had held talks with Tehran on deporting Iranians during the war.

The France-Iran cyberattack story broke on November 9, with French officials blaming Iran for an 'unprecedented' hack on supermarket refrigerators across Europe over the past month and vowing retaliation. This added a new, almost absurdly domestic, front to the conflict. Meanwhile, Russia deepened its ties with Iran through a missile-launcher deal, and Iran's security chief met Putin to deliver a message from Khamenei. The G7 ministers gathered in Paris to press Rubio on Iran. Iran's IAEA report showed it hardening its line against nuclear monitoring. The overall mood in Tehran was one of cautious triumph at the US political setback mixed with the grinding reality of a war that had not yet ended.

The most likely trajectory for the coming week is a tense, grinding stalemate with low-intensity friction continuing in the Strait of Hormuz and no major escalation or major deal. Here is my theme-by-theme assessment.

Diplomacy and the peace process: It is probable that Qatar-mediated talks will continue in a slow, back-and-forth rhythm. Trump will keep saying a deal 'could happen' while Rubio publicly grumbles about Iran's demands. Iran will hold firm on its conditions, particularly around nuclear monitoring and the end of the naval blockade. I would rate a formal ceasefire or signed agreement by November 16 as unlikely, though possible if Trump feels the political pressure from the new Democratic Congress is becoming too loud. A two-day intensive talks session, which Iran proposed, might be scheduled, but I would not bet on it producing a breakthrough. Confidence: probable that talks continue, unlikely that a deal is signed.

Strait of Hormuz and maritime friction: Almost certain that at least one or two more tanker or shipping incidents will be reported in the strait over the next week. Iran has shown a pattern of hitting one or two ships, claiming a US or Israeli link, and then pausing. The US task force targeting land supply routes will likely produce at least one reported interception or strike near the Iraq border. Iran may test the new US land blockade by attempting to move cargo through alternative corridors. I expect the strait to remain partially disrupted, with insurance premiums high and some shipping lines still routing around. Confidence: almost certain for at least one incident, probable for continued partial disruption.

US domestic politics and pressure on Trump: Probable that House Democrats will introduce or advance some form of war-powers resolution or spending restriction aimed at the Iran war. The shutdown-risk story will keep simmering. Hegseth will likely face at least one major press confrontation or a written question from the new House majority. The impeachment chatter will grow louder in Democratic ranks but I would not expect a formal vote to be scheduled within this one-week window. Trump will keep walking the line between 'we are not at war' and 'I could strike again if they push me.' Confidence: probable for Congressional pressure to intensify, possible for a formal war-powers vote to be announced, unlikely for an impeachment resolution to be introduced this week.

France and the fridge hack: Possible that France will announce a specific retaliatory measure, whether a sanctions package, a cyber counter-strike, or a diplomatic note of protest. This is a new front and could briefly dominate the news cycle, but I expect it to remain a secondary story to the main US-Iran track. Confidence: possible for a French response to be announced, unlikely for it to trigger a new military dimension.

Iran's domestic politics and security: Probable that the security crackdown will continue, with at least one or two more arrests or short-term detentions of students, clerics, or journalists reported. The executions of the three men from the January protests will be used by the opposition and the diaspora as a rallying point. The IRGC's underground construction and the lifted missile-range limit will be cited in military briefings. I would not expect a major protest or street uprising to break out within this week, but the simmering discontent is there. Confidence: probable for continued low-level repression, unlikely for a major protest wave.

Oil and markets: Oil will remain volatile, likely trading in the $85-to-$95 range, with sharp daily swings tied to any headline about Hormuz or talks. The weekly decline since 2020 that just closed will set the tone. If even one more tanker is hit, expect a 3-to-5 percent intraday spike. If talks are reported as 'making progress,' expect a 2-to-3 percent dip. The Bank of England and other central banks will keep the Iran war in their inflation commentary. Confidence: almost certain for continued volatility, probable for oil to stay below $100.

Russia-Iran axis: Possible that the missile-launcher deal will produce a visible delivery or a joint training exercise within the week. Iran's security chief's meeting with Putin signals a closer alignment, and I expect at least one more high-level contact. This will be framed in the West as a concern but will not change the immediate military calculus. Confidence: possible for a visible Russia-Iran military step, unlikely for a new joint operation.

Nuclear program and IAEA: Iran's hardened line against monitoring in its IAEA report will likely prompt a statement from the IAEA director-general and a few Western capitals. The $20 million US reward will keep generating headlines. I would not expect a new IAEA inspection or a major nuclear-site strike within this week. Confidence: probable for diplomatic friction over monitoring, unlikely for a physical nuclear event.

Less-likely surprises I would keep on my radar: France carrying out a visible cyber counter-strike that causes a minor outage in Iranian infrastructure; a surprise US strike on a new Iranian target if a tanker crew is killed; the new House Democrats scheduling a war-powers vote for the following week and announcing it this week; Iran briefly closing the Strait of Hormuz to all traffic for 24 to 48 hours as a bargaining chip; a second wave of executions or a mass trial being announced.

So the US president, who wanted to look tough, now has to be more careful. He can't just keep bombing without Congress agreeing to pay for it. This means the war will slow down a bit in the US, but it is not over.

In the ocean between Iran and the rest of the world, called the Strait of Hormuz, Iran keeps hitting ships with small bombs and mines. The US is sending more boats to protect the ships. It is like a game of cat and mouse that has been going on for weeks. Next week, more ships will probably get hit, and the US will probably respond. It is not a big battle, but it is constant and it makes oil prices go up and down.

At the same time, Qatar is trying to get the two sides to talk. Iran sent a proposal about its nuclear program. The US said it is close to a deal but then said Iran's demands are too big. So the talks are happening, but they are slow. Nobody thinks a real deal will be signed next week. But the talks will keep going, and that is what keeps both sides from doing something really big.

A few other things are happening too. France got hacked in a weird way — someone messed with supermarket refrigerators across Europe, and France blames Iran. Russia and Iran are getting closer, with a deal about missile parts. And inside Iran, the government is getting stricter: more arrests, more underground bunkers being built, and more executions. The overall feeling is that Iran is preparing for a longer fight, while the US is trying to figure out how to end it without looking weak.
