measurement.happened:
This week in Israel was dominated by one enormous political event and a cluster of secondary crises that made it feel like the country was being shaken on multiple axes at once.

The central story, supported by nearly every single source, was the aftermath of Israel's legislative election and the president's decision to hand the mandate to form a government to Gadi Eisenkot rather than to Benjamin Netanyahu. President Isaac Herzog accepted the election results on November 4, opened consultations with parties, and on November 7 officially tasked Eisenkot, the leader of the anti-Netanyahu bloc, with building a coalition. Reuters, AP, AFP, BBC, CNN, DW, TV5Monde, Bloomberg, WSJ, FT, and Al Jazeera all covered this in detail. Eisenkot immediately called for a 'wide' government and said he was open to Netanyahu himself joining the cabinet, a remark that Al Jazeera and Reuters both highlighted. The Joint List, the main Arab party bloc, confirmed on November 5 that it would back Eisenkot, and a veteran Arab lawmaker told AP he was willing to break with the long-standing precedent of not sitting in a Jewish-led government. Bloomberg reported that Eisenkot had 67 potential backers, while Netanyahu lost the historical support of one ultra-orthodox party, according to TV5Monde. The path is anything but smooth: multiple sources, including Bloomberg, WSJ, and Al Jazeera, stressed that the opposition is internally divided and that Eisenkot's task is genuinely tough. Netanyahu, meanwhile, pressed hard on his claim that the election was stolen, specifically that Arab voters had been manipulated. The poll chief publicly rebuked him (FT, November 2), the attorney general traded barbs with him (Reuters, November 2), and on November 9 the Shin Bet reported it found no evidence of foreign election meddling, a finding Al Jazeera reported that directly undercuts Netanyahu's fraud narrative. Netanyahu and his attorney general continued to trade accusations, and the overall tone was one of a bitter, unresolved contest in which the loser is not yet accepting the result.

The second major theme was the seismic shift in the US-Israel relationship, triggered by the US midterm elections on November 3. Trump, on Election Day, announced that the United States would stop providing approximately 4 billion dollars in annual military aid to Israel by the end of the year, saying 'they don't need it.' This was covered by virtually every source: Reuters, AP, BBC, CNN, DW, TV5Monde, Bloomberg, WSJ, and FT. The Israeli president was described by CNN as being 'shocked,' calling it 'like a bolt from the blue.' Bloomberg ran multiple pieces on how Israel risks missing how quickly US support is evaporating, and noted that JD Vance broke with Trump on the Iran and Israel questions, blaming the Iran war and Israel ties for the GOP's midterm rout. WSJ ran an exclusive on the billions of dollars in pending defense orders that complicate a clean end to aid. The broader context, as Bloomberg and WSJ framed it, is that the US-Israel alliance is confronting its biggest test in decades, and the Democratic sweep of Congress means pro-Israel members of the party will face internal pressure. Trump himself said on November 9, per CNN, that his 'great dislike' for Israel contributed to Republican losses, a remarkable admission that Al Jazeera and Bloomberg both picked up.

The third theme was the Gaza humanitarian crisis, which took on a new and visceral dimension this week because of heavy rains. Tens of thousands of displaced Palestinians living in tents were flooded out. A sand embankment collapsed onto tents on November 9, killing four or five people, including children, as reported by Reuters, BBC, Al Jazeera, and TV5Monde. Al Jazeera ran a series of vivid pieces: 'Tents don't protect us,' photos of displacement camps collapsing under rainwater, Gaza turning discarded cooking pots into seawalls, and building wind turbines out of rubble. A mass wedding of 250 couples in Gaza (BBC, Al Jazeera) offered a small counterpoint of life persisting. Israeli strikes still killed people in the early part of the week (AP, November 1: eight killed including a child). The overall picture is of a population in a prolonged state of displacement, with the rainy season now adding a new layer of danger on top of the war's destruction.

A fourth, smaller thread ran through the week: settler activity and the West Bank. Settlers moved into Palestinian homes in Israeli-occupied Jericho, displacing dozens, and Palestinians protested (Reuters, Al Jazeera, November 5-6). Israel also closed Hebron's Ibrahimi Mosque to Palestinians for a Jewish holiday (Al Jazeera, November 6), and was reported tightening its grip on Palestinian schools in East Jerusalem. These are incremental but they feed the broader identity and territorial tensions that the election has put in the spotlight.

A fifth thread was the military and regional dimension. Israel built a 90-kilometer network of military roads across southern Lebanon (Al Jazeera, November 7), and Lebanese civilians were reported packing bags and stocking up amid fears of a new Israeli escalation (Al Jazeera, November 6). Netanyahu pressed Trump for renewed strikes against Iran (FT, November 2), the Gulf was braced for escalation (FT, November 2), and a bomb threat prompted checks on an Israel-bound cruise ship in a Greek port (Reuters, November 3). CNN noted that 60 years of denial about Israel's nuclear weapons program was confronting a new reality. These threads suggest the security environment remains tense and that the new government, whoever forms it, will inherit a region on edge.

Finally, there were international reactions that signal a broader shift in global mood toward and away from Israel. Tens of thousands marched in Amsterdam in a 'Red Line' protest pressing the Dutch government on Gaza (AP, Al Jazeera, November 8-9). A US city voted to divest from Israel (Al Jazeera, November 6). Mélenchon promised action against Israeli annexation if elected president (Al Jazeera, November 7). A council may withdraw from Israel-linked investments (BBC, November 4). These are not yet policy changes, but they are a barometer of the growing international pressure that the new Israeli government will face.
measurement.expected:
For the week of November 9 through roughly November 16, the following is my read, theme by theme.

Government formation and coalition talks. This is the story that will define the week. Eisenkot has been formally tasked, and in the Israeli system he now has a window (typically up to 42 days, but the first few weeks are critical) to build a working majority. I am almost certain that formal coalition negotiations will begin within the next two or three days, involving the Joint List, the centrist and left-leaning parties that backed Eisenkot, and possibly one or two smaller factions from the Netanyahu camp. The key question is whether Eisenkot can lock in enough seats. Bloomberg reported 67 potential backers, which is a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, but 'potential' is doing a lot of work in that number. I judge it probable that at least one round of substantive talks will happen, and possible that a rough framework will be outlined by the end of the week. I am less certain about whether a deal will be signed; the internal divisions in the opposition, flagged by Al Jazeera and BBC, are real. Eisenkot's openness to Netanyahu joining is a clever move to reduce the opposition's unity, but it also risks making his own camp uneasy. I would say there is a real chance, maybe 40 to 50 percent, that by November 16 we still do not have a confirmed government, and the story becomes one of extended, messy negotiations.

Netanyahu's response. I am almost certain that Netanyahu will continue to contest the result in some form. The Shin Bet finding of no foreign meddling (Al Jazeera, November 9) undercuts his strongest external argument, but his core claim is about domestic Arab voting patterns, which is harder to disprove in the public eye. I expect him to keep trading barbs with the attorney general and the poll chief, to make public statements that keep his base agitated, and to test whether any of his coalition partners will wobble. There is a possible, though not probable, scenario in which he attempts a confidence vote or some procedural maneuver in the Knesset to test the new government's numbers. I would not bet on him formally resigning or calling for a snap recount within this one-week window, but I would not rule out a dramatic press conference or a Knesset speech that sets up a fight for the following weeks.

US-Israel relations and the aid question. The Trump announcement is now on the record, and the Democrats control Congress. I am almost certain that the aid issue will dominate the diplomatic agenda. Expect statements from the Israeli finance and defense ministries, possibly a request for an emergency meeting with US officials, and a lot of back-channel phone calls. The WSJ exclusive on pending defense orders suggests the cut is not as clean as it sounds, and I expect that technical wrangling to continue. I am probable that the Israeli government, whoever is forming it, will issue a public statement expressing concern or surprise, and that the Israeli shekel and bond markets will show some jitters. I am possible that there is a first round of talks between the incoming government's foreign ministry (or the foreign minister-designate) and the US State Department within the week. I would not bet on a full reversal of the aid decision or a dramatic US-Israel summit in this short window, but the conversation will be loud and public.

Gaza and the humanitarian picture. The rains are not going to stop on schedule. I am almost certain that the flooding and its aftermath will continue to be a major news story, with more casualties, more displaced families losing shelter, and more international pressure on Israel to allow aid in. The sand embankment collapse on November 9 will likely prompt an inquiry or at least a public response from the Israeli military. I am probable that the new government formation process will force Eisenkot's team to start thinking about Gaza policy, and that there will be early signals about whether the new government intends to change the tempo or scope of operations. I am possible that there is a minor escalation in the West Bank, given the settler activity in Jericho and the general tension, but I would not bet on a full-scale flare-up in this specific week.

Lebanon and the broader security front. The 90-kilometer military road network in southern Lebanon is a significant infrastructure move, and I am probable that it will generate fresh Lebanese and UNIFIL complaints. I am possible that there is a minor cross-border incident, a skirmish, or a flare-up in the north, but I judge a full-scale re-escalation of the Israel-Lebanon front as unlikely in this one-week window unless something triggers it. The Iran question, with Netanyahu pushing for renewed strikes and Vance breaking with Trump, keeps the Gulf on edge, but I would not bet on a new US-Israeli strike on Iran within seven days.

Less likely surprises (things I could see but would not bet on): a sudden resignation or internal collapse in one of Eisenkot's key coalition partners, throwing the math into chaos; a dramatic Netanyahu press conference in which he formally challenges the result in the Supreme Court; a major new strike or incident in Gaza that shifts the entire political conversation; the shekel dropping sharply on the back of the aid news and the political uncertainty; a surprise back-channel deal between the US and the incoming Israeli government that partially walks back the aid cut.

Things I would not bet on: Eisenkot announcing a fully formed, sworn-in government by November 16 (the math is too tight and the talks too fresh); a full confidence vote in the Knesset that topples the new government before it is even formed; a major military operation in Lebanon or a new wave of strikes on Iran within this week; the shekel collapsing or the Israeli stock market crashing more than a few percent; a formal US-Israeli summit or state visit in this specific week; a new national security incident or terrorist attack in Israel that reshapes the political calculus.

Overall, my sense is that this will be a week of intense political theater, a lot of talking and posturing, some genuine negotiation behind closed doors, and a background hum of humanitarian crisis in Gaza. The government question will not be fully resolved, but the direction is now clearly away from Netanyahu, and that is the most important fact about the week ahead.

delta.motion:
The single biggest shift between the two photographs is the movement from political paralysis to political action. On November 1, Israel was frozen in a deadlock: no winner, no mandate, Netanyahu claiming the vote was stolen, analysts guessing whether a second election was coming. By November 9, the president had officially tasked Eisenkot with forming a government, the Joint List had confirmed it would back him, and the question had changed from 'who gets to try?' to 'can Eisenkot actually pull this off?' That transition compressed what might have been a month of uncertainty into a single week of concrete horse-trading.

The US-Israel relationship grew from a background note to a front-burner crisis. In the first photograph, Trump was 'preparing for Iran escalation ahead of the polls' and the alliance was assumed stable. In the second, Trump has announced a $4 billion annual aid cut, called Israel's support 'not needed,' admitted his 'great dislike' for Israel contributed to Republican midterm losses, and JD Vance has broken with him on the Iran question. This is not a tweak; it is a structural renegotiation of the relationship that had been taken for granted.

The Gaza story grew in visceral human cost but shrank in military escalation. The first photograph showed new strikes, a killed Hamas commander, and a truce under stress. The second photograph shows the truce still holding in military terms but the rainy season arriving: a sand embankment collapsing onto tents and killing children, displacement camps flooding, cooking pots turned into seawalls. The war's physical violence did not spike, but the weather added a new, almost cruel layer to an already broken population. The mass wedding of 250 couples is a small but telling counterpoint: life persisting inside the crisis.

Netanyahu's fraud narrative grew in specificity and then hit a wall. In the first photograph he was 'attacking the result' and blaming 'foreign entities.' In the second, the poll chief publicly rebuked him, the attorney general traded barbs, and the Shin Bet reported finding no evidence of foreign meddling. The narrative did not vanish, but it lost its most powerful prop. Meanwhile, the crypto/sanctions debate and the Polymarket suspicious-trades investigation, both prominent on November 1, have largely faded from the headlines, suggesting the market has moved on to the bigger story of US aid.

The West Bank thread continued but shifted in texture. The dramatic Hebron siege of 5,000 displaced people gave way to smaller but equally telling moves: settlers moving into Jericho homes, the Ibrahimi Mosque closed to Palestinians for a Jewish holiday, East Jerusalem schools under tighter grip. The scale is smaller, but the direction is the same: incremental tightening of control.

New themes appeared that were absent from the first photograph. The 90-kilometer network of military roads being built across southern Lebanon is a physical, long-term commitment to a military posture that signals Israel does not see the Lebanon border as settled. The 60-year nuclear denial entering public conversation is a new chapter in how Israel's ultimate deterrent is perceived. The cruise ship bomb threat in a Greek port is a small but concrete reminder that the security perimeter extends beyond the region. The Amsterdam 'Red Line' march, a US city voting to divest, and Mélenchon's annexation promise show the international pressure broadening from cultural boycotts (Eurovision, Lorde) to more substantive political and financial moves.

What shrank or vanished: the specific cultural boycott stories (Eurovision, Swiss bobsled, Lorde) receded. The 'teenage innovators reusing rubble' human-interest angle faded. The 'Jewish ex-cop representing an Islamist party' detail dropped out of the narrative. The specific 'AI image of Arab voters' controversy that sparked backlash in the first week is no longer in the headlines. These were symptoms of the election moment; once the election was over and the mandate was handed out, they lost their urgency.

What came that was not expected is the most important miss. The US midterm elections on November 3 and Trump's $4 billion aid cut were not in the forecast at all. The first photograph mentioned Trump 'preparing for Iran escalation ahead of the polls,' but the forecast did not connect the US political calendar to Israel's next week. The aid cut, the 'bolt from the blue' reaction from the Israeli president, the JD Vance break, and the Democratic sweep of Congress are a cluster of events that fundamentally changed the external environment Israel faces. The rainy season in Gaza was also not in the forecast. The expectation focused on military strikes and truce stability, but the weather added a humanitarian dimension that is now as newsworthy as the strikes themselves. The forecast was a security-and-politics forecast; the reality was also a weather-and-society forecast. The pattern of error is not that the forecast was wrong about Israel's internal politics, but that it was too narrow in its lens, treating the country as an isolated system rather than one embedded in a shifting US political environment and a Mediterranean climate.
delta.driver: The force pushing Israel from the first photograph to the second is the collision of three compressed timelines that are now running simultaneously. The first is the internal political clock: Eisenkot has a constitutional deadline to form a government, and every day he fails to do so pushes Israel closer to a second election, which Netanyahu believes he can win. This creates a race in which the new prime minister must balance Arab party support, ultra-orthodox defections, and his own party's internal fractures while the old prime minister digs in with a fraud narrative that the Shin Bet has just undermined. The second is the external US clock: Trump has announced a $4 billion aid cut by year's end, and the pending defense orders that WSJ identified mean the money is not just a line item but a web of contracts, relationships, and strategic assumptions that must be renegotiated. The 'great dislike' Trump expressed is not a mood; it is a policy lever, and the new Israeli government will be formed in the shadow of a US that is actively deciding how much it still wants to pay for the relationship. The third is the Gaza clock: the rainy season has arrived, the tents are failing, and the humanitarian situation is deteriorating on a timeline that is not governed by coalition math or US politics but by weather and the physical limits of a population living in the open. These three timelines do not wait for each other. Eisenkot must form a government while the US is cutting the check and the rain is falling on Gaza. The country is being pushed from a state of post-election confusion into a state of simultaneous management, where the new government's first act will not be a policy speech but a triage of three crises that are all accelerating at once.

crystal.eli5:
Imagine you just won a really close election, but you need to team up with a bunch of other people to actually run the show. That's what's happening in Israel right now. A guy named Eisenkot just got the job of building a team (a government) out of all the different political parties. He has a deadline, and everyone is watching to see if he can pull it off. The hardest part is that the people he needs to work with don't always agree with each other, and the guy he beat (Netanyahu) is still mad and saying the election was rigged.

At the same time, the United States, which used to be Israel's biggest backer in money and weapons, just said it's going to stop giving about four billion dollars a year. The president of the US basically said he doesn't really like Israel right now. That's like your best friend suddenly saying they're not going to share their lunch with you anymore. Everyone in Israel is a little shocked and trying to figure out what to do.

And in Gaza, where a lot of people are still living in tents because their homes were destroyed, it started raining hard. The tents are not great at keeping out water, and one of the walls holding back the rain actually collapsed on top of people sleeping in tents, and a few kids were hurt. It's like being stuck outside in a storm where your shelter is made of cardboard. The weather is making an already really hard situation even harder, and the pictures of people trying to keep their heads dry are making the news all over the world.

So the next week is going to be about three things happening at the same time: trying to build a government, trying to figure out what the US is going to do, and trying to keep people alive in the rain. None of them are easy, and none of them wait for the other two to be finished.

display.eli5:
Imagine you just won a really close election, but you need to team up with a bunch of other people to actually run the show. That's what's happening in Israel right now. A guy named Eisenkot just got the job of building a team (a government) out of all the different political parties. He has a deadline, and everyone is watching to see if he can pull it off. The hardest part is that the people he needs to work with don't always agree with each other, and the guy he beat (Netanyahu) is still mad and saying the election was rigged.

At the same time, the United States, which used to be Israel's biggest backer in money and weapons, just said it's going to stop giving about four billion dollars a year. The president of the US basically said he doesn't really like Israel right now. That's like your best friend suddenly saying they're not going to share their lunch with you anymore. Everyone in Israel is a little shocked and trying to figure out what to do.

And in Gaza, where a lot of people are still living in tents because their homes were destroyed, it started raining hard. The tents are not great at keeping out water, and one of the walls holding back the rain actually collapsed on top of people sleeping in tents, and a few kids were hurt. It's like being stuck outside in a storm where your shelter is made of cardboard. The weather is making an already really hard situation even harder, and the pictures of people trying to keep their heads dry are making the news all over the world.

So the next week is going to be about three things happening at the same time: trying to build a government, trying to figure out what the US is going to do, and trying to keep people alive in the rain. None of them are easy, and none of them wait for the other two to be finished.

This week in Ukraine was dominated by a brutal cycle of Russian strikes on energy infrastructure and civilian targets, Ukraine's escalating campaign against Russian oil refineries, and the final diplomatic preparations for US-brokered peace talks in Abu Dhabi. Let me walk through the major threads.

**Russian strikes on energy and civilian targets (the dominant story).** Russia launched what multiple sources described as massive overnight missile and drone barrages on Kyiv and surrounding regions, hitting power substations, a major bridge, and logistics infrastructure. Hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians lost electricity, and Kyiv was plunged into darkness. Zelensky and the Kyiv mayor publicly traded blame over the city's blackout, which added a layer of domestic political friction. In the south, a Russian strike on an aid center in Zaporizhzhia killed at least 53 people (the toll kept climbing from 26 to 31 to 40 to 53 across multiple reports), making it one of the deadliest single attacks of the war. A hospital, a hospice, and a school used as an aid shelter were also hit. Russia also targeted emergency crews responding to the strike, which Kyiv called a double-tap attack, and shared bodycam footage. Zelensky warned that Russia's strikes are designed to cut Ukraine in half. The cumulative effect is that steel production shut down, grain exports stalled, and the economy is being choked. (Supported by: Reuters Nov 6-9, AP Nov 2-9, BBC Nov 1-9, CNN Nov 3-8, DW Nov 1-9, TV5Monde Nov 1-9, Bloomberg Nov 3-9, FT Nov 9, Al Jazeera Nov 3-9, CNBC Nov 1.)

**Ukraine's counter-strikes on Russian refineries and logistics.** Ukraine hit at least six Russian oil refineries in the span of the week, including Saratov, Ryazan, and Yanos, plus a hub of the e-retailer Ozon in southern Russia. Zelensky confirmed the campaign is continuing. The result is visible: Russia is rationing petrol in several regions, shipping metal via the Arctic to evade Ukrainian strikes, and its diesel is reportedly going unsold. This is Ukraine's most effective economic lever this year, and it is clearly designed to squeeze Russia just before the talks. (Supported by: Reuters Nov 4-9, Bloomberg Nov 3-9, FT Nov 9, Al Jazeera Nov 5-6, CNBC Nov 1.)

**Abu Dhabi talks and the Trump-Melania diplomatic push.** The US announced it will mediate trilateral talks between the US, Ukraine, and Russia in Abu Dhabi the following week. Russian diplomats and military officials confirmed they will attend. European foreign ministers, including France's Kallas, said they will join. Trump met Putin's top envoy at the White House and called the prospective deal 'big and beautiful.' Melania Trump hosted both Russian and Ukrainian delegations at the White House, positioning herself as an 'exclusive intermediary' on a local ceasefire and calling for a 'more enduring' truce. Zelensky awarded Melania a state honour and expressed gratitude. The talks are expected to focus on security guarantees for both sides. (Supported by: Reuters Nov 2-9, AP Nov 2-9, BBC Nov 5-9, CNN Nov 3-7, DW Nov 5-9, TV5Monde Nov 5, Bloomberg Nov 2-9, FT Nov 7-8, Al Jazeera Nov 3-9, CNBC Nov 3.)

**US midterms and the 'Blue Wave.'** The November 3 US midterm elections produced a Democratic sweep in Congress. Ukraine bonds jumped on the news. Zelensky said Ukraine must adapt to new US political realities and hopes the Democratic Congress will bring more aid and scrutiny of Russia. Analysts framed it as a potential shift in US foreign policy on Ukraine, Iran, and Israel. The Kremlin, meanwhile, expressed hope that the election shake-up would not shift Trump's negotiating posture. (Supported by: Reuters Nov 4-6, CNN Nov 4-6, DW Nov 4, TV5Monde Nov 4, Bloomberg Nov 4, FT Nov 7, Al Jazeera Nov 5, CNBC Nov 4.)

**Cyber warfare and information attacks.** Both Ukraine and Russia reported that their emergency alert apps were hacked, with fake nuclear attack warnings issued to civilians on both sides. Hacked records revealed an estimated 400,000 Russian military deaths. Pro-Russian hackers targeted Italy's foreign minister. A Belarusian source claimed to have obtained data on Russian losses. The information war is clearly intensifying alongside the kinetic one. (Supported by: Reuters Nov 6, AP Nov 2, BBC Nov 2, DW Nov 2-3, TV5Monde Nov 1, Bloomberg Nov 2, CNBC Nov 2.)

**Kherson ceasefire ends, fighting resumes.** The longest localized ceasefire of the war, in the Olechky/Kherson sector, ended around November 1-2. Civilians prepared for the return of heavier Russian attacks. The ceasefire had been brokered with Melania Trump's involvement, and its end is a blow to the diplomatic narrative. (Supported by: Reuters Nov 1, BBC Nov 1-2, DW Nov 2, TV5Monde Nov 2, Al Jazeera Nov 1.)

**European diplomacy and funding fights.** The G7 foreign ministers met in Paris, pressing US Secretary Rubio on Ukraine and Iran. Germany's Merz threatened to block the EU budget over Ukraine funding and issued an ultimatum. Meloni warned Europe risks irrelevance in the peace talks and criticized the EU's 'disjointed' approach. Italy shipped fresh military aid despite a coalition split. Germany proposed an extra 100 million euros for Ukrainian infrastructure. A first multinational military exercise for a potential postwar Ukraine force was held in Poland. Ukraine's EU membership path is lagging behind Moldova's. (Supported by: Reuters Nov 5-9, AP Nov 9, BBC Nov 3, DW Nov 3-9, TV5Monde Nov 5, Bloomberg Nov 5-9, FT Nov 5, 7, 9, Al Jazeera Nov 6.)

**IMF and financial support.** The IMF launched a loan review that could unlock 1.67 billion dollars for Ukraine. Donors at a Paris meeting promised half the funding for repairing the Chernobyl arch. The US pushed to restore Russian gas sales to Europe via Ukraine, a move that will be politically sensitive in Kyiv. (Supported by: Reuters Nov 9, TV5Monde Nov 9, WSJ Nov 2.)

**Domestic political friction and corruption.** Zelensky publicly criticized the SBU security service over a corruption scandal. Senior security and police officials were accused of running a criminal ring. A military recruitment dorm saw clashes. Zelensky and the Kyiv mayor traded blame over the blackout. These are signs of internal strain under wartime pressure. (Supported by: Reuters Nov 5-7, BBC Nov 3.)

**Military and strategic developments.** Russia is reportedly using its own version of Starlink for military communications over Ukraine. Ukraine is adapting to Russian jet-powered drones. Russian land gains are dwindling while its army suffers record losses, with 350 conscripts killed in a single period. Palantir is harvesting battlefield data that Ukraine pays for 'with blood.' Finland is considering Ukraine-style tank barriers. (Supported by: Reuters Nov 6, DW Nov 7, TV5Monde Nov 6, Bloomberg Nov 2, Al Jazeera Nov 5-6, FT Nov 7.)

Looking at the week of November 9 through roughly November 16, here is what I expect, theme by theme, with my confidence level.

**Abu Dhabi trilateral talks (almost certain).** The US, Ukraine, and Russia will sit down in Abu Dhabi, with European diplomats joining. This was announced multiple times this week, delegations are confirmed, and both sides have been striking hard in the days before, which is classic pre-talks posturing. The agenda will center on security guarantees, the scope of any ceasefire, and whether a broader 'all of Europe' deal is on the table. I expect the talks to produce a joint communique or a framework document, but not a signed peace agreement. Zelensky has already flagged that the security deal floated by Trump could be 'potentially dangerous,' so there will be friction. Russia will likely insist on no concession on territory. I rate the talks happening as almost certain, producing a tangible document as probable, and producing a full ceasefire deal as possible but not probable.

**Continued Russian strikes on energy (almost certain).** Russia has been hitting power infrastructure daily this week and Zelensky warned of more strikes on energy targets, bridges, and infrastructure. With winter heating season approaching and the talks happening, Russia has both the motive (pressure) and the means (missiles, drones) to keep striking. I expect at least one major overnight barrage on Kyiv or surrounding regions during the week, leaving hundreds of thousands without power. Confidence: almost certain.

**Ukraine's refinery campaign continues (probable).** Ukraine has hit six refineries in a week and Zelensky confirmed the campaign is ongoing. Russia is already rationing fuel. I expect at least one or two more Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries or logistics hubs, particularly in the Volga region or southern Russia. This is Ukraine's most effective economic weapon and it would be odd to pause it during talks. Confidence: probable.

**Post-talks diplomatic scramble (almost certain).** Whatever comes out of Abu Dhabi will trigger a cascade of statements from Trump, Zelensky, Putin, Meloni, Merz, Kallas, and others. I expect a mixed reception: Western allies pushing for a stronger European role, Russia testing the waters, and Ukraine trying to lock in security guarantees. The G7 meeting in Paris this week will set the European tone. Confidence: almost certain that there is a flurry of diplomatic statements and follow-up meetings.

**IMF review progresses (probable).** The IMF launched its review on November 9. These processes typically take a few weeks, but I expect staff-level consultations to begin or be ongoing during this period. The 1.67 billion dollar unlock is not immediate but the process is now in motion. Confidence: probable that the review is actively underway; almost certain that it is not yet concluded.

**Winter heating crisis becomes more acute (probable).** With hundreds of thousands already without power, heating season is here, and Russian strikes are targeting the grid, I expect growing public complaints, possible localized rationing of electricity in some regions, and Zelensky or regional governors making public appeals for generators and emergency aid. The Madrid summit appeal for energy infrastructure aid will gain urgency. Confidence: probable.

**Cyber incidents continue (possible).** The alert app hacks and the 400,000-casualty data leak show both sides are active in cyberspace. I expect at least one more notable cyber incident, possibly targeting energy SCADA systems, government websites, or another round of fake alerts. Confidence: possible.

**European military preparation (probable).** The first multinational exercise in Poland has started. I expect additional training exercises, logistics planning, and political discussions about the composition and mandate of a potential postwar European force in Ukraine. This is a long-term project but the groundwork is being laid now. Confidence: probable that planning and exercises continue; unlikely that a full deployment decision is made this week.

**Domestic political friction (possible).** The SBU corruption scandal, the recruitment dorm clashes, and the Zelensky-mayor blame game suggest internal tensions are rising. I expect at least one more public spat or a minor reshuffle in the security apparatus, but not a full-blown crisis. Confidence: possible.

**US congressional dynamics (probable).** The new Democratic Congress will likely hold early hearings or issue statements on Ukraine aid, possibly pushing for Patriot systems or a more structured aid package. Zelensky's comment about solving the 'Patriot air defence issue' suggests this is a live negotiation. Confidence: probable that the new Congress makes noise about Ukraine in its first days.

**Less likely surprises I would watch for:**
- A sudden Russian proposal to extend the Kherson ceasefire as a goodwill gesture before or after Abu Dhabi (possible but not probable).
- A major Ukrainian drone or missile strike on a Russian capital or a high-profile target like Moscow or St. Petersburg as a pre-talks signal (possible).
- A second cyberattack on critical Ukrainian infrastructure, such as a bank or a hospital network (possible).
- Zelensky making a surprise visit to Washington or Brussels to meet the new Congress or EU leaders in person (possible).
- A minor escalation in the Black Sea, such as a naval engagement or a mine incident, given Russia hit three ships this week (possible).

**Things I would not bet on:**
- A full ceasefire or peace agreement being signed in Abu Dhabi (unlikely; both sides are still far apart, and the 'no concession' framing from Al Jazeera suggests hard positions).
- A major ground offensive by either side in a new sector (unlikely; both are focused on the talks and the energy war).
- Zelensky resigning or a major cabinet reshuffle (unlikely; the corruption scandal is serious but not yet at that level).
- A nuclear incident or a shift in the nuclear dimension of the war (unlikely; no signs of that in the headlines).
- A full EU membership decision for Ukraine (unlikely; the process is slow and the FT notes Ukraine is behind Moldova).
- A major natural disaster or a new pandemic hitting Ukraine specifically (unlikely).

delta.driver: The force pushing Ukraine from the first photograph to the second is the collision of two clocks: the military clock of winter and the diplomatic clock of Abu Dhabi. Russia is trying to break Ukraine's energy infrastructure before the cold deepens, because a population without power in December is a population that is harder to defend and harder to keep fighting. Ukraine is trying to squeeze Russia's economy through its refinery campaign, because a Russia that is rationing petrol and shipping metal over the Arctic is a Russia that enters the talks with a tighter budget and a more urgent need for a deal. Both sides are, in effect, raising their stakes in the two weeks before the trilateral meeting, knowing that whatever they achieve on the ground will set the floor for what they will accept at the table. The US midterm elections added a third clock: a Democratic Congress that is more likely to scrutinize Russia and press for aid, which changes the political arithmetic in Washington and gives both Kyiv and Moscow a new reason to move quickly or to stall. Melania Trump's self-appointed role as intermediary, Zelensky awarding her a state honor, and the White House hosting both delegations are not just diplomatic theater; they are the US trying to own the process before a new Congress can reshape it. The underlying driver, then, is a race: both sides are trying to maximize their position in the kinetic domain while the diplomatic domain is being assembled, and the winter season is the deadline that makes the race urgent. Everything else, the cyber attacks, the corruption scandal, the Black Sea, the EU budget fight, is downstream of that central competition between the front and the table.

The Zaporizhzhia aid-center strike that killed 53 people will generate a wave of political and legal follow-up: European foreign ministers will issue statements, the UN-backed war-crimes inquiry will likely file a new report or add the incident to its docket, and Kyiv will share the bodycam footage of the double-tap in a coordinated media push. Zelensky's warning that Russia is trying to 'cut Ukraine in half' will be echoed in European capitals. The cumulative economic damage, with steel production shut down and grain exports stalled, will be quantified in new reports. I expect the blackout in Kyiv to persist for several days, generating domestic frustration and possibly a new round of Zelensky-mayor friction over restoration efforts. The strikes are not just military; they are a diplomatic weapon, designed to make Ukraine more desperate at the table and to make the European partners more sympathetic to a quick deal.

UKRAINE'S REFINERY CAMPAIGN AND RUSSIA'S ENERGY SQUEEZE (high confidence of continuation; medium confidence of a tactical pause during talks): Ukraine has hit at least six Russian refineries in the past week, and Russia is visibly feeling it: petrol rationing in several regions, metal being shipped via the Arctic to evade Ukrainian drones, diesel going unsold. This is Ukraine's most effective economic lever this year. I expect the campaign to continue, but there is a realistic chance of a brief tactical pause during the Abu Dhabi talks themselves, as both sides would want to signal flexibility. If the talks produce a framework, the pause may extend for a few days. If the talks produce little, the campaign will resume with even greater intensity, possibly targeting refineries closer to Moscow or St. Petersburg. The US push to restore Russian gas sales to Europe via Ukraine is a politically sensitive thread that will generate friction in Kyiv, especially with a new Democratic Congress watching. This is a contradiction Ukraine must manage: it is squeezing Russia's oil sector militarily while Washington wants to reopen the gas pipeline diplomatically. I expect Zelensky to publicly acknowledge the US proposal while privately pushing back, and for the new Democratic Congress to use the issue to assert its oversight role. The refinery campaign is not just a military operation; it is a negotiating position, and its tempo will be calibrated to the diplomatic calendar.

CYBER WARFARE AND THE INFORMATION FRONT (medium-high confidence of at least one more incident; medium confidence of it becoming a headline): Both sides' emergency alert apps were hacked this week, with fake nuclear attack warnings sent to civilians. Hacked records revealed an estimated 400,000 Russian military deaths. Pro-Russian hackers targeted Italy's foreign minister. This is a new and growing front that the previous forecast underweighted. I expect at least one more cyber incident this week, possibly timed around the Abu Dhabi talks to create pressure, confusion, or a pretext for a side to claim the other is not in good faith. The 400,000 deaths figure will be the subject of a media war: Russia will contest the number, Ukraine and its allies will try to verify it through independent sources, and the figure will be used in the talks as a marker of Russian losses. The hacked alert apps will generate public frustration on both sides and may lead to a temporary switch to SMS or radio alerts. I expect at least one European official to make a public statement about the cyber attacks, linking them to the broader information war. The cyber front is not a side story; it is a parallel battlefield that will shape the tone of the talks and the public perception of each side's credibility.

US DOMESTIC POLITICS AND THE NEW CONGRESS (medium confidence of visible congressional activity; low confidence of a major policy shift): The Democratic sweep in the November 3 midterms is a new variable that the previous forecast completely missed. The new Congress is in its first weeks and will be asserting its oversight role. I expect at least one Ukraine-related headline from Washington this week: a hearing, a statement from the new Senate or House leadership, or a question about the Abu Dhabi process. The Democratic Congress is more likely to scrutinize Russia and press for aid, which changes the political arithmetic in Washington. Ukraine bonds jumped on the midterm results, and I expect them to continue benefiting from the new political climate. However, Trump is still President, and the new Congress will not be able to unilaterally reshape policy in its first week. The effect is more about tone and pressure than about concrete legislative action. I expect the new Congress to use the Abu Dhabi talks as a test case for its oversight role, with at least one Democratic senator or representative making a public statement about the process. The US push to restore Russian gas sales via Ukraine will be a point of congressional friction, with Democrats potentially questioning why the US is re-opening a pipeline to Russia while also squeezing Russia's oil sector. The midterm effect is real but gradual; it will shape the next several months more than this single week.

DOMESTIC POLITICAL FRICTION IN UKRAINE (medium confidence of continued headlines): Zelensky publicly criticized the SBU security service over a corruption scandal involving senior officers, traded blame with the Kyiv mayor over the capital's blackout, and a military recruitment dorm saw clashes. The wind tells me I have been underweighting this. I expect the corruption scandal to generate at least one more headline this week, possibly involving a new arrest, a parliamentary question, or a public statement from a senior official. The blame game over the blackout will continue as restoration efforts are slow and the cold deepens. Zelensky faces the challenge of projecting unity and confidence for the Abu Dhabi talks while managing internal dissent. The recruitment dorm clashes are a small but telling sign of strain in the military's social fabric. I expect Zelensky to make at least one public statement addressing domestic concerns, possibly framing the corruption fight as a sign of strength rather than weakness. The domestic friction is not a crisis, but it is a recurring source of headlines that will complicate the narrative of a unified Ukrainian delegation at the talks.

EUROPEAN DIPLOMACY AND FUNDING (medium confidence of at least one headline; low confidence of a major decision): Germany's budget ultimatum over Ukraine funding, the G7 pressure on US Secretary Rubio, the IMF loan review that could unlock $1.67 billion, and the first multinational military exercise for a potential postwar Ukrainian force are all active threads. The wind tells me European stories tend to fade faster than I expect. I expect at least one European funding or diplomatic headline this week, but I should not bet on a major EU decision. The IMF review is a slow process; the $1.67 billion will not be unlocked this week, but the review itself will generate a headline. The Chernobyl arch funding round, with donors promising half the cost, is a smaller, more concrete item that may generate a follow-up. The multinational military exercise in Poland will produce a report or a statement, but it is a background item. Germany's budget ultimatum is the most likely to generate a headline, as Merz has threatened to block the EU budget over Ukraine funding. I expect at least one European foreign minister to make a public statement linking the Abu Dhabi talks to European security guarantees. The EU membership path for Ukraine remains slow, and I do not expect a major step this week.

MILITARY AND STRATEGIC DEVELOPMENTS (medium confidence of at least one headline): Russia is reportedly using its own version of Starlink for military communications over Ukraine. Ukraine is adapting to Russian jet-powered drones. Russian land gains are dwindling while its army suffers record losses, with 350 conscripts killed in a single period. Palantir is harvesting battlefield data. Finland is considering Ukraine-style tank barriers. These are quieter but strategically significant developments. I expect at least one of these to generate a headline this week. Russia's satellite network is a structural development that will become more visible as the war drags on. The jet-powered drones are a new threat that Ukraine is still adapting to, and I expect at least one incident involving them. The Russian losses figure will be contested and used in the information war. Palantir's data harvesting is a behind-the-scenes development that may generate a corporate or defense-industry headline. Finland's tank barriers are a smaller, more concrete item that may generate a European defense headline.

WHAT I WOULD NOT BET ON: A full peace deal or comprehensive ceasefire signed in Abu Dhabi. A major Ukrainian ground offensive capturing a Russian-held city. A dramatic US congressional vote on Ukraine aid levels in the first week of the new Congress. Russia pulling back from any front or making a major territorial concession. A nuclear or chemical incident. Zelensky resigning or being removed from power. A full EU membership treaty for Ukraine. A major Black Sea naval incident involving a sinking or a collision. A new African or Asian country announcing troop deployment to Ukraine. A full resolution of the SBU corruption scandal. A complete restoration of Kyiv's power grid within the week. A second-city ceasefire brokered by Melania Trump that holds for more than a few days. A formal US government inquiry into the Starlink issue. A new wave of Ukrainian strikes on Russian targets within 100 km of Moscow (though a strike within 200 km is possible).

emoji_reasons: The US-brokered trilateral peace talks in Abu Dhabi are the defining event of the week, with both sides entering from positions of maximum pressure and a new Democratic Congress watching.

Russia's escalating strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure, including the 53 killed in Zaporizhzhia and Kyiv's blackout, continue to dominate the military narrative and set the stakes for the talks.

Ukraine's sustained campaign against Russian oil refineries, with six hit in a week and Russia rationing petrol, is the most effective economic lever in the war and will shape the diplomatic calculus.
crystal.tldr: The Abu Dhabi trilateral talks between the US, Ukraine, and Russia are the central event of the week, with both sides entering from positions of maximum pressure after a week of record Russian strikes and Ukraine's most aggressive refinery campaign yet. Expect a framework or process agreement rather than a full deal, continued Russian strikes on energy infrastructure, at least one cyber incident, and the new Democratic Congress beginning to assert its oversight role. The talks will be read through the lens of winter's approaching deadline and the new US political reality.
crystal.eli5:
Next week, the big thing is a meeting in Abu Dhabi where the US, Ukraine, and Russia sit down together to try to talk about peace. Both sides are trying to look strong before the meeting: Russia has been bombing Ukraine's power plants really hard, and Ukraine has been bombing Russia's oil factories. Think of it like two kids about to share a toy, and each one is trying to show the other they can break it first.

The meeting will probably not end with a perfect peace deal. More likely, they will agree to keep talking, maybe pause fighting in one small area, and write down some ideas. That is actually normal for this kind of meeting. The new US Congress, which now has more Democrats, will be watching closely and probably asking questions about whether the deal is fair for Ukraine.

Meanwhile, the war keeps going. Russia will probably keep bombing power plants because it is getting cold and they want Ukraine to be more desperate. Ukraine will probably keep hitting Russian oil factories because it is their best way to make Russia feel the pain. There will also be more hacking and fake alerts on phones, which is a new kind of fighting that is getting worse.

The main thing to watch is whether the meeting produces something real, even if it is small, or whether it just produces a lot of photos and a statement that says 'we will keep talking.' Either way, it is the most important thing happening in Ukraine next week.

measurement.happened: This week in North Korea was dominated by three intertwined storylines that together painted a picture of a regime on the offensive, both militarily and rhetorically. The single biggest story was the Binance cryptocurrency heist. The FBI publicly accused North Korea of being behind the record 6.3 billion dollar theft, the largest crypto heist in history, and every major outlet from Reuters and AP to Al Jazeera, CNBC, Bloomberg, the Wall Street Journal, Deutsche Welle, TV5Monde, and the BBC covered the accusation and the North Korean denial. Pyongyang called the US charge a trite provocation and evidence of a hostile policy, and the BBC ran a major Global Story feature on November 9 about how the heist was pulled off. Bloomberg added that North Korean hackers are now weaponizing AI in their operations, and the Financial Times noted the stolen billions will take months to launder. Binance itself said outflows had normalized, and North Korea's own state media pointed to the hack as proof that the United States is not a trustworthy partner. A secondary but related thread was North Korea's condemnation of a financial task force for keeping the country on a crime blacklist, which Reuters reported on November 5. The second major storyline was an intense burst of weapons testing. In roughly a week, North Korea test-fired an air-defence missile, staged a cruise missile drill, and conducted a strategic cruise missile test with a dispersal warhead, making it the fourth weapons launch in a single month. Bloomberg reported the testing pace is now twice what it was during Trump's first term, and the Wall Street Journal called it the busiest missile-testing spree in years. Kim Jong Un toured a large warship and ordered shipyard upgrades, and CNN reported on a new drone war machine. The US-South Korea nuclear drill in early November was cited by Pyongyang as further proof that a stronger nuclear deterrent is needed. The third storyline was diplomacy. Trump's midterm setback, referenced across Reuters, AFP, and Bloomberg, dimmed hopes for a US-North Korea summit. North Korea told the world it had no reason to dialogue with a hostile United States, yet stopped short of closing the door, saying talks remain an option. The Wall Street Journal noted Pyongyang was rebuffing Trump's diplomacy. In Beijing, senior Chinese and North Korean officials met and urged closer ties, signaling the DPRK is leaning further toward its traditional ally. The EU got told to mind its own business by Deutsche Welle, and the overall diplomatic tone was one of guarded openness mixed with pointed irritation. On the domestic front, state media touted a BBQ restaurant boom that sceptics dismissed as propaganda, and a decade-old broadcast was mistakenly circulated as an announcement of Kim Jong Un's death, which Pyongyang had to walk back, as the BBC reported on November 9.
measurement.expected: Binance hack fallout: I would say it is almost certain that at least one more official North Korean statement referencing the hostile policy or the provocation will appear in the coming days, likely routed through KCNA or a foreign ministry note. The FBI and US Treasury may add names to sanctions lists or issue further indictments, and the laundering of the stolen billions will continue in the background as the Financial Times suggested. The BBC's November 9 feature will keep the story in the news cycle through at least mid-November. Confidence: almost certain for further rhetoric, probable for a new US sanction or indictment. Missile and weapons testing: Given the pace of four launches in a month and the framing of the busiest testing spree in years, I would expect at least one more missile or drone test in the coming week, possibly a short-range ballistic missile or another cruise missile shot toward the Sea of Japan. A fifth test in the same month is consistent with the pattern. Confidence: probable, roughly 65 to 70 percent. US diplomacy: Trump, still processing his midterm results, may make a public gesture or a social-media post aimed at Kim. North Korea will likely respond with a mix of we are open and you are hostile. A full summit is unlikely in this window, but a back-channel signal through China is possible. Confidence for some diplomatic signal: possible. Confidence for a meeting or summit: unlikely. China channel: The Beijing meeting suggests a closer coordination period. Expect North Korea to route some of its diplomatic messaging through China, and possibly a follow-up working-level meeting or a joint statement on trade or security. Confidence: probable. Domestic propaganda: The BBQ restaurant story and the death-rumor correction suggest state media will keep pushing positive domestic narratives. Expect more achievements coverage, possibly a new construction project, a sports event, or a Kim Jong Un inspection tour of a factory or military unit. Confidence: almost certain. EU and financial blacklist: North Korea may issue a follow-up complaint to the EU or the financial task force. Not a major headline, but a small statement is possible. Confidence: possible. Less likely surprises: A surprise intermediate-range ballistic missile test would be a big escalation but is possible. A sudden Kim Jong Un health scare or an unexplained absence from official photos is possible, especially given the death-rumor incident this week. A joint North Korean-Chinese naval exercise announced within the week is possible. North Korea accepting a back-channel US overture and hinting at a meeting is unlikely but not impossible. Things I would not bet on: A full US-North Korea summit in the next seven days. A major underground or atmospheric nuclear test. A sudden regime change or succession announcement. North Korea inviting a large group of foreign journalists on a tour. A ceasefire or de-escalation framework with South Korea.

delta.motion:
The Binance heist grew from a single FBI accusation into a full-cycle story: Pyongyang issued a formal denial calling the charge a trite provocation, the BBC produced a major Global Story feature dissecting the mechanics, Bloomberg added that North Korean hackers are now weaponizing AI, the Financial Times noted the stolen billions will take months to launder, and Binance confirmed outflows had normalized. A related new thread appeared: North Korea publicly condemned a financial task force for keeping the country on a crime blacklist, which Reuters reported on November 5. This is a slightly different register than the hack itself, but it shows the financial-pressure storyline expanding beyond a single incident into a broader grievance about international finance.

Weapons testing grew the most visibly. The first photo showed ten ballistic missiles and a drone exhibition. The second photo shows an air-defence missile test, a cruise missile drill, and a strategic cruise missile with a dispersal warhead, making it the fourth launch in a single month. The Wall Street Journal called it the busiest missile-testing spree in years, and Bloomberg said the pace is now twice what it was during Trump's first term. A naval dimension appeared that was not in the first photo: Kim Jong Un toured a large warship and ordered shipyard upgrades. The drone war machine from the first photo is still present but no longer the headline; the cruise missile and the warship are the new center of gravity.

Diplomacy shifted in tone. The first photo showed Kim's China trip and the new bridge as a warm, forward-looking gesture. The second photo shows senior Chinese and North Korean officials meeting and urging closer ties, which is consistent, but it is paired with a sharper posture toward the West: North Korea told the world it had no reason to dialogue with a hostile United States, the EU was told to mind its own business, and Trump's midterm setback dimmed summit hopes. The door is not closed, but the tone is more pointed and irritated than the first photo's cautious optimism.

Several threads from the first photo shrank or vanished. The Swiss diplomatic channel, which had produced a rare foreign minister visit, does not appear in the second photo at all. The Russia-North Korea labor pipeline, which had been a quiet but important economic thread, also disappears from the second photo's coverage. The landmine border row and the UN letter accusing South Korea of fabricating the incident have faded from the headlines, suggesting the two sides managed the row down without a new incident. The succession whispers that the Wall Street Journal had flagged are replaced by a small, almost comic hiccup: a decade-old broadcast was mistakenly circulated as an announcement of Kim Jong Un's death, which Pyongyang had to walk back, as the BBC reported on November 9. This is not succession news, but it shows how fragile the information environment around the leadership still is.

New elements appeared that were not in the first photo: the financial blacklist condemnation, the naval shipyard upgrade order, the strategic cruise missile with a dispersal warhead, the AI-weaponization angle from Bloomberg, the state media touting of a BBQ restaurant boom that sceptics dismissed as propaganda, and the Trump midterm setback as a diplomatic headwind. The overall motion is from a week defined by a single massive cyber event and a missile barrage to a week defined by a sustained multi-domain weapons cadence, a sharper diplomatic posture, and the slow maturation of the Binance story into a longer financial and reputational fight.
delta.wind:
On the Binance aftermath, the expectation was almost exactly right. The FBI attribution did trigger a wave of follow-up reporting, and North Korea did deny involvement through state media, calling the charge a trite provocation, which matches the predicted "deny or stay conspicuously silent" path. The US did not launch a full-blown diplomatic crisis, confirming the "unlikely" call. The Swiss channel, which was expected to produce a small tangible output, went quiet, a minor miss. On internal and succession whispers, the expectation of a small media cycle about Kim's health or the next generation was partially met in an unexpected form: the mistaken death-broadcast circulation and the walk-back are a small signal of information-environment fragility, but they are not succession news. The no-actual-change call was correct. The BBQ restaurant boom is a new domestic color that was not in the expectation set, though it is minor.

On the less-likely surprises, the new underwater or hypersonic weapon did not appear, but the strategic cruise missile with a dispersal warhead is in the same family of "new weapon that catches attention." The Trump-Kim call or meeting did not happen, but the Trump midterm setback is a new factor that was not in the original expectation and that dimmed the already-low probability. The second cyber-attack did not materialize. The internal unrest signal did not appear, though the death-broadcast mix-up is a small adjacent blip.

The things not bet on were all correctly not bet on: no war, no nuclear test, no foreign visit by Kim, no change of government, no unilateral sanctions lift.

The pattern of misses is telling. The expectations captured the right themes and the right direction but undercounted the intensity of the weapons testing and the sharpness of the diplomatic tone. The secondary economic threads (Switzerland, Russia labor) were expected to produce at least a small output and produced none, suggesting that in a week dominated by the Binance story and the testing cadence, quieter diplomatic and economic channels get crowded out of the news cycle. The expectations also did not anticipate the naval dimension, the AI-weaponization angle, or the financial blacklist thread, all of which are natural extensions of the main stories but were not explicitly predicted. The overall error is one of underestimating the regime's willingness to escalate the military signal and sharpen the rhetorical posture in the same week, rather than managing the two tracks separately as the expectation implicitly assumed.
delta.driver: The central force pushing North Korea from the first photograph to the second is the Binance heist acting simultaneously as a windfall, a provocation, and a test of the sanctions architecture. The six-billion-dollar crypto theft gave the regime a huge lump sum of hard currency that traditional sanctions struggle to capture, which emboldens it to spend on weapons and shipyard upgrades while it also gave the US a concrete grievance to press, which in turn pushed Pyongyang to sharpen its rhetorical posture and signal that it is not a country that negotiates under pressure. Trump's midterm setback complicated the diplomatic window: the US leader is still open to talks but is less politically able to make a quick deal, and North Korea read that as a reason to be less accommodating, saying it has no reason to dialogue with a hostile United States while keeping the door technically open. The US-South Korea nuclear drill in early November gave Pyongyang a fresh security-dilemma justification for the cruise missile and air-defence tests, and the testing cadence itself became a self-reinforcing signal: each launch validates the next one in the regime's internal logic. China's steady presence, from the new bridge to the senior-level meeting, provides a stable backstop that lets Pyongyang be more assertive toward the West without feeling exposed on its eastern flank. The underlying driver, then, is a regime that has just collected a historic windfall, is being publicly accused of it, is watching its main diplomatic counterpart get politically weaker, and is responding by spending more on military capability, talking tougher, and leaning harder into Beijing, all while keeping just enough diplomatic oxygen to avoid a full break.

measurement.happened:
This week in Venezuela was dominated by a natural disaster that shook the country literally and figuratively, set against a backdrop of a remarkable diplomatic thaw with the United States and a slow, messy economic reopening.

THE EARTHQUAKE AND ITS AFTERMATH. By far the most dramatic story of the week was the earthquake. Deutsche Welle reported on November 6 that Venezuela was hit by its strongest quakes in more than a century. CNN followed up on November 8 with the grim finding that construction flaws had been discovered in the housing towers that collapsed during the quakes, suggesting that a significant share of the deaths and injuries was not just bad luck but bad building. This is a huge story for a country where public housing has long been a political symbol and where corruption in construction contracts is a persistent grievance. Expect the government to face intense pressure to explain why buildings failed, and opposition figures to use the disaster to highlight years of neglected infrastructure. The emotional and political fallout will ripple well into the next week.

US-VENEZUELA DIPLOMATIC PUSH AND ELECTION PRESSURE. The second major thread is the clear, sustained US push to get Venezuela onto a democratic track. Reuters reported on November 2 that Secretary of State Rubio spoke with a Venezuelan minister about reforms that lay groundwork for elections, and a second Reuters piece the same day described Rubio meeting his Venezuelan counterpart as the US pressed for progress on election preparations. Al Jazeera ran two pieces on November 3 describing the US urging Venezuela to follow a phased plan for democratic transition. BBC added on November 3 that Rubio specifically urged Venezuela to release the remaining political prisoners. Bloomberg noted on November 3 that the US and Venezuela were in talks on a fresh aluminum cargo as part of a broader trade revival. The Washington Post, via WSJ on November 4, framed the shift in security cooperation: Venezuela, once a haven for guerrillas, is now helping the US attack them. Altogether this paints a picture of a US that has moved from maximum pressure to a carrot-and-stick engagement model, trading economic reintegration and security cooperation for concrete democratic steps. This is a significant shift from the 2019-2023 era.

POLITICAL PRISONERS AND DOMESTIC REFORMS. María Corina Machado, the opposition figure who has become the moral center of Venezuelan politics, renewed her call for the release of political prisoners outside a Venezuelan prison on November 6, per AP. The WSJ ran an opinion piece on November 1 calling Machado a source of new hope. On the legislative side, Bloomberg reported on November 3 that Venezuela moved to unwind the hate speech law that had jailed thousands, a concrete legal step that signals the government is trying to clean up the most controversial instruments of its authoritarian toolkit. These two threads together suggest the government is making real, if cautious, concessions under US pressure.

OIL, ENERGY, AND THE PRIVATE SECTOR. The oil sector had a busy week. Reuters reported on November 3 that oil exports were unchanged amid stagnant output and high freight rates, while Bloomberg noted on November 2 that a freight surge had pushed exports to an eight-month low. On the positive side, Reuters reported on November 2 that GeoPark entered Venezuela under a 25-year deal with Colombia's Gilinski taking control, and Bloomberg followed on November 6 with GeoPark assessing logistics and liabilities at the Venezuelan oil field ahead of the takeover. Bloomberg also painted a vivid picture on November 3 of the oil rush bringing private jets and soaring rents to a frontier town, capturing the gold-rush atmosphere as foreign capital returns. The energy sector is clearly a central pillar of the reintegration story.

POWER OUTAGES AND DAILY LIFE. Reuters reported on November 5 that Venezuelans protested power outages, a reminder that the electricity grid remains fragile and that daily life is still marked by shortages. The same theme of economic strain shows up in Reuters' November 2 note that Christmas decorations were muted compared to previous years, a small but telling detail about the mood of the population.

REGIONAL AND OTHER THREADS. Reuters noted on November 3 that the foreign ministers of Brazil and Venezuela discussed trade and Amazon cooperation, a sign of South American re-engagement. The Financial Times ran a brief item on November 9 about IESA, the prestigious Caracas business school, hinting at institutional activity in the capital. The overall picture is of a country in a transitional, fragile, but genuinely more open moment than it has been in years, with the earthquake as the week's defining shock.

A significant change in the exchange rate or a new currency announcement.

The most dramatic change between the two photographs is the arrival of a story that was not present at all in the first one: the earthquake. On November 6 Venezuela experienced its strongest quakes in over a century, and by November 8 CNN was reporting that construction flaws in the collapsed housing towers meant a significant share of the deaths was due to bad building, not just bad luck. Machado is still there, still pressing for political prisoners and elections, but she is now one thread in a broader tapestry rather than the single face on the front page. The return drama shrank; the ongoing substance of her work grew.

In the first photograph it was mostly about oil: the first tanker in Texas, Chevron's output targets, the 51st-state quip, the Swiss engineering deal. By the second photograph, the relationship had broadened into a full diplomatic engagement. Rubio was holding talks with Venezuelan ministers about election reforms, urging the release of political prisoners, and the Washington Post was reporting a genuine shift in security cooperation, with Venezuela helping the US attack guerrillas. The oil thread continued but its character changed: instead of a single headline deal, we now see a broader private-sector rush, with GeoPark entering under a 25-year deal, private jets landing in a frontier oil town, rents soaring, and simultaneously freight costs pushing exports to an eight-month low. The story moved from one transaction to an ecosystem.

Several themes from the first photograph vanished or shrank to near-invisibility. The 51st-state talking point, the specific Swiss engineering contract, the Weatherford and Eni drilling details, the PDVSA bonds court ruling, the cocoa pest, Judge Hellerstein's death, the Colombia border bomb blast, and the Guyana border ruling all dropped out of the headlines. The three-actor drama of Machado versus Rodríguez versus the US, which was the organizing frame of the first week, became less visible as a head-to-head confrontation and more visible as a layered, multi-issue negotiation.

What came true: Machado continued her domestic push, held events, and pressed for concrete steps. The expectation listed as possible a major oil sector disruption such as a PDVSA worker strike or a technical failure at a key refinery. The freight surge and eight-month export low were a strain, but not a dramatic disruption.

What came that was not expected, and this is the important part: The earthquake. The expectation explicitly listed a major earthquake or natural disaster under things it would not bet on. And yet it was the single most dramatic story of the week, dominating headlines, generating follow-up reporting on construction flaws, and reshaping the political conversation about infrastructure and corruption. The muted Christmas decorations were a small human detail that the expectation did not picture. GeoPark's specific 25-year deal with Gilinski taking control was a concrete new entry that the expectation only vaguely anticipated with its note about possible new contracts.

What this says about our expectations: We were too locked into the political three-actor frame of Machado, Rodríguez, and the US, and we underweighted the physical and institutional fragility of the country. The earthquake, the power outages, the construction flaws, the muted Christmas, the freight costs, the worker shortages, the grid repairs, these are the texture of daily Venezuelan life, and they kept intruding on the political narrative. We correctly identified the diplomatic thaw and the oil sector momentum, but we treated the country as if it were primarily a political story with economic underpinnings, when in reality the economic and physical infrastructure is so fragile that it constantly threatens to override the political narrative. We also overestimated the likelihood of dramatic confrontational moments between Machado and Rodríguez and underestimated the likelihood of quiet, incremental legislative and diplomatic steps. The expectation's tone of cautious optimism mixed with real tension was broadly right, but the earthquake added a layer of vulnerability and urgency that the political frame alone could not capture. In short, we expected a political week and got a physical one with politics layered on top.
delta.driver: The force pushing Venezuela from the first photograph to the second is the collision between an external reintegration process and an internal physical and institutional fragility that years of mismanagement have accumulated. The US, under Trump and Rubio, has opened a window of engagement that trades economic reintegration, security cooperation, and diplomatic normalization for concrete democratic steps, and that window is generating real activity in oil, trade, and legislation. But the window is narrow, and the country's physical infrastructure, its power grid, its housing stock, its construction quality, its freight costs, its worker shortages, is so degraded that it keeps interrupting the political narrative with reminders of how much has been neglected. The earthquake was not a surprise in the geological sense, but it was a political earthquake because it exposed the gap between the optimism of the diplomatic thaw and the reality of buildings that should not have collapsed. Machado is the moral center of the political story, but the population's daily experience of outages, muted Christmases, and bad construction is the gravitational force that keeps pulling the narrative back from the three-actor drama to the question of whether the country can actually function. The US is the external engine, the Rodríguez government is the cautious negotiator trying to concede just enough to keep the window open, and the physical reality of the country is the constraint that no amount of diplomacy can override. The driver, in short, is a country trying to modernize its political and economic institutions at the same speed that its physical infrastructure is breaking down, with the US providing both the incentive and the pressure to move faster than the ground can hold.

measurement.happened: This week in Canada was dominated by the ongoing US-Canada trade war and the government's fiscal response to it. Prime Minister Mark Carney tabled his second federal budget, which leaned heavily on higher oil revenues to fund tax incentives, infrastructure spending, and a push to reduce Canada's economic dependence on the United States. The budget included billions for housing (relaxing the foreign buyer ban), a one-time measure granting permanent status to 200,000 temporary residents, reforms to bank ownership rules to stoke competition, and a dedicated homelessness fund. Carney framed the budget as a sovereignty play, and the government explicitly stated that the US midterm results would not change Canada's trade stance. The budget drew immediate criticism from markets, with the Canadian dollar posting its worst week since September and traders trimming rate-hike bets after unemployment climbed to a six-month high of 6.7 percent. The Bank of Canada, under Governor Macklem, renewed its framework around the 2 percent inflation target and pledged to proceed carefully on further rate increases, while the Ivey PMI edged higher but manufacturing slipped into contraction territory. On the trade front, the week opened with Trump declaring the US was close to a deal with Canada and Carney confirming progress, but by week's end the picture was murkier: Trump's cabinet makers faced a doubling of his tariff, Canadian oil traded at its widest discount to US prices since 2018, and Canada Goose reported a widening loss on higher costs. The US midterm election, which produced a Democratic victory, was met with genuine relief in Ottawa, and Democrats in Congress began hatching a plan to reverse Trump's Canada tariffs. Simultaneously, Canada deepened ties elsewhere: it extended its tariff deal with China, China announced debut yuan and green bond sales in the Canadian market, and the EU and Canada moved closer toward a formal association agreement. The US Treasury also sanctioned eight Canadian money-services firms over Iran-related transactions, adding a layer of friction to an already strained relationship. In a major institutional move, Carney recruited Bridgewater's co-CIO Karniol-Tambour to lead Canada's sovereign wealth fund, a signal that the government intends to build a long-term fiscal buffer. The week also saw a dramatic sports-political collision: Canada barred Russia and Belarus from the upcoming IIHF World Junior Ice Hockey Championships, defying a court ruling and triggering threats of a six-country boycott. Norway complained it had been bumped by the IIHF to make room for Russia, and the uncertainty cast a shadow over the tournament. Meanwhile, at the IIHF Women's World Championship, Canada dominated, routing Japan 9 to 0 and easing past Sweden. A tragic incident in the west saw a mother and daughter killed in a suspected multi-grizzly attack, sparking calls for better wildlife management. In the territories, the Francophonie summit put the Canadian armed forces and the French-speaking north in the spotlight, with Yellowknife hosting military exercises and the Northwest Territories featuring prominently in coverage of francophone life. On the corporate side, RBC announced its acquisition of Yarra Capital, the National Bank acquired Embark Student Corp, Blackstone led a 3.1 billion dollar investment in LNG Canada, Foodtastic offered 720 million dollars for MTY Food, and Sherritt furloughed 47 percent of its Canadian workforce over Cuba sanctions. A Wall Street battle over Canada's plan to build a rival to Musk's Starlink also threatened to upend the project. In Alberta, the premier faced growing backlash after winning a referendum to remain in Canada, a vote that was supposed to settle separatist questions but instead reopened old wounds. The Canada-India 5.5 billion dollar bank takeover continued to draw opposition from workers and politicians. All told, it was a week of fiscal ambition, trade anxiety, hockey politics, and a government trying to prove it can steer Canada away from its biggest trading partner while the dollar weakens and jobs tighten.
